## Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Research")]

Inventions by University of Minnesota students and faculty have ranged from food science to health technologies. Most of the public research funding in Minnesota is funneled to the University of Minnesota as a result of long-standing advocacy by the university itself.

The university developed [Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopher_(protocol) "Gopher (protocol)"),[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-105) a precursor to the [World Wide Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web") which used [hyperlinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlinks "Hyperlinks") to connect documents across computers on the internet. However, the version produced by [CERN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN") was favored by the public since it was freely distributed and could more easily handle multimedia webpages.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-106) The university also houses the [Charles Babbage Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Babbage_Institute "Charles Babbage Institute"), a research and archive center specializing in computer history. The department has strong roots in the early days of supercomputing with [Seymour Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Cray "Seymour Cray") of [Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cray "Cray") supercomputers.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-107)

The university also became a member of the [Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Interferometer_Gravitational-wave_Observatory "Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory") (LIGO) in 2007 and has led data analysis projects searching for gravitational waves — their existence [was confirmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_observation_of_gravitational_waves "First observation of gravitational waves") by scientists in February 2016.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-timeshighereducation.com-32)

Discoveries and innovation by faculty or alumni include:

*   [Puffed rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puffed_rice "Puffed rice") – [Alexander P. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_P._Anderson "Alexander P. Anderson") performed work leading to the discovery of "puffed rice", a starting point for a new breakfast cereal later advertised as "Food Shot From Guns".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-108)
*   Transistorized cardiac pacemaker – [Earl Bakken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bakken "Earl Bakken") founded Medtronic, where he developed the first external, battery-operated, transistorized, wearable artificial pacemaker in 1957.
*   [Green Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution "Green Revolution") – [Norman Borlaug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Borlaug "Norman Borlaug") was an agronomist who led initiatives worldwide that contributed to extensive increases in agricultural production termed the Green Revolution. Borlaug, often called "the father of the Green Revolution", is credited with saving over a billion people worldwide from starvation. Borlaug was awarded multiple honors for his work, including the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom"), and the [Congressional Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Gold_Medal "Congressional Gold Medal").
*   [ATP synthase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATP_synthase "ATP synthase") – [Paul D. Boyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_D._Boyer "Paul D. Boyer") elucidated the enzymatic mechanism for synthesis of the cellular "energy currency", [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") (ATP), leading to a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1997.
*   [Point-contact transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-contact_transistor "Point-contact transistor") – [Walter Houser Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Houser_Brattain "Walter Houser Brattain") and [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen"), later joined by [William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley "William Shockley"), invented the point-contact transistor in December 1947. For their invention, the trio was awarded a [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") in 1956.
*   [Infusion pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infusion_pump "Infusion pump") – [Henry Buchwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Buchwald "Henry Buchwald") invented the world's first infusion port, peritoneovenous shunts, and specialty vascular catheters. He also invented the first implantable infusion pump, a precursor to implantable infusion pumps in use throughout the world today.
*   [Photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis") – [Melvin Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Calvin "Melvin Calvin") discovered the [Calvin cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_cycle "Calvin cycle") along with Andrew Benson and James Bassham; for this, he won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
*   [Ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecology "Ecology") – [Raymond Lindeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Lindeman "Raymond Lindeman") revolutionized ecology, primarily through his 1942 paper "Trophic Dynamic Aspect of Ecology", which described how energy and nutrients cycled through ecosystems.
*   [Supercomputer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer") – [Seymour Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Cray "Seymour Cray") designed a series of computers that were the fastest in the world for decades, and founded Cray Research, which built many of these machines.
*   [Taconite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taconite "Taconite") – [Edward Wilson Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Wilson_Davis "Edward Wilson Davis") developed an engineering process to economically extract iron ore from hard taconite rocks, making taconite valuable as iron ore for the iron and steel industries.
*   [Cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays "Cosmic rays") – [Phyllis S. Freier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllis_S._Freier "Phyllis S. Freier") discovered the presence of heavy nuclei in cosmic rays, proving the similarity between the Solar System and the rest of the galaxy.
*   U.S. aviation – [Robert Rowe Gilruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rowe_Gilruth "Robert Rowe Gilruth") led the development of flying qualities for airplanes, the use of rockets to achieve data at supersonic speeds, and the establishment of many of the nation's leading flight research and human space flight operations facilities.
*   [Bone marrow transplant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_marrow_transplant "Bone marrow transplant") – [Robert A. Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Good "Robert A. Good") in 1968 performed the first successful human bone marrow transplant between persons who were not identical twins and is regarded as a founder of modern immunology. In 2018 Minnesota Gov. [Mark Dayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dayton "Mark Dayton") proclaimed August 24 as University of Minnesota Blood and Marrow Transplant Day.
*   [Gore-Tex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gore-Tex "Gore-Tex") – [Robert Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_W._Gore "Robert W. Gore") invented Gore-Tex materials in 1969.
*   [Disk drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_drive "Disk drive") – [Reynold B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynold_B._Johnson "Reynold B. Johnson") invented a method and machinery to score tests electronically.
*   [K-rations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-rations "K-rations") – [Ancel Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancel_Keys "Ancel Keys") developed the rations for the U.S. military and also conducted dietary studies: the Minnesota Starvation Study and the Seven Countries Study.
*   [Synthetic rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_rubber "Synthetic rubber") – [Izaak Kolthoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izaak_Kolthoff "Izaak Kolthoff") developed the "cold process" for producing synthetic rubber, which he undertook under the U.S. synthetic rubber program during World War II.
*   [Cyclotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotron "Cyclotron") – [Ernest Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lawrence "Ernest Lawrence") won the Nobel Prize for Physics 1939 for inventing and developing the cyclotron.
*   _[Drosophila melanogaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila\_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster")_ – [Edward Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_B._Lewis "Edward B. Lewis") won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995 for his work on the _Drosophila_ bithorax complex of homeotic genes.
*   [Cardiac surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_surgery "Cardiac surgery") – [C. Walton Lillehei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Walton_Lillehei "C. Walton Lillehei") pioneered open-heart surgery, as well as numerous techniques, equipment, and prostheses for cardiothoracic surgery.
*   [POPmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/POPmail "POPmail") – [Mark P. McCahill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_P._McCahill "Mark P. McCahill") led the development of the Gopher protocol, the effective predecessor of the World Wide Web; was involved in creating and codifying the standard for Uniform Resource Locators (URLs); and led the development of POPmail, one of the first e-mail clients, which had a foundational influence on later e-mail clients and the popularization of graphical user interfaces in Internet technologies more broadly.
*   [MMPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Multiphasic_Personality_Inventory "Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory") – [Starke R. Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starke_R._Hathaway "Starke R. Hathaway") and [J. C. McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._McKinley "J. C. McKinley") created the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), which was first published in 1943.
*   [Zatocoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zatocoding "Zatocoding") – [Calvin Mooers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Mooers "Calvin Mooers") developed a mechanical system using superimposed codes of descriptors for information retrieval called Zatocoding, 1948.
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Edward P. Ney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_P._Ney "Edward P. Ney") discovered cosmic ray heavy nuclei and solar proton events. After early work involving separating isotopes from uranium, he worked on the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project").
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Alfred O. C. Nier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_O._C._Nier "Alfred O. C. Nier") devised a method to isolate the isotopes of uranium, a critical discovery in the atomic age. Nier worked with [Kellex Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellex_Corporation "Kellex Corporation") in New York City on the design and development of efficient and effective mass spectrographs for use in the Manhattan Project to build the atomic bomb in World War II. He designed most of the spectrographs used for monitoring uranium separations during the war.
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Frank Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Oppenheimer "Frank Oppenheimer") worked on uranium isotope separation in 1945 and joined the Manhattan Project.
*   [Biotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology "Biotechnology") – [Ronald L. Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_L._Phillips "Ronald L. Phillips") was the first to generate whole corn plants from cells grown in culture, which laid the foundation for, and sparked, a new industry using cell-culture methods to genetically modify corn plants and other cereals. The corn cell line most widely used for genetic modification of corn has greatly accelerated the improvement of corn as food, feed, and fuel.
*   [Renewable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") – [Lanny D. Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanny_D._Schmidt "Lanny D. Schmidt") designed a reactor to extract hydrogen from ethanol, offering the first real hope hydrogen could be a source of inexpensive and renewable energy.
*   [Biomimetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomimetics "Biomimetics") – [Otto Schmitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Schmitt "Otto Schmitt") invented the Schmitt trigger, the cathode follower, the differential amplifier, and the chopper-stabilized amplifier.
*   [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") – [Deke Slayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deke_Slayton "Deke Slayton") was one of the original NASA Mercury Seven astronauts and became NASA's first chief of the Astronaut Office. He served as NASA's director of flight crew operations, making him responsible for crew assignments at NASA, from November 1963 until March 1972. At that time, he was granted medical clearance to fly and was assigned as the docking module pilot of the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, at age 51 becoming the oldest person to fly in space at the time.
*   [Bathythermograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathythermograph "Bathythermograph") – [Athelstan Spilhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athelstan_Spilhaus "Athelstan Spilhaus") fully developed the bathythermograph (BT) in 1938, an instrument he perfected that was of vital importance in World War II against the German U-boat. During the war, the BT became standard equipment on all U.S. Navy subs and vessels involved in antisubmarine warfare.
*   [CDC 6600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDC_6600 "CDC 6600") – [James Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_E._Thornton "James E. Thornton") developed the CDC 6600, the world's first supercomputer, designed with Seymour Cray.
*   [Ziagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziagen "Ziagen") – [Robert Vince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Vince_(scientist) "Robert Vince (scientist)") worked on antiviral drug candidates at UMN, where he went on to develop carbocyclic nucleosides termed 'carbovirs.' This class of medicinal agents included the drug abacavir. Abacavir was commercialized by GlaxoSmithKline as Ziagen for the treatment of AIDS.
*   US3D[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-109) – Graham Candler[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-110) pioneered the future of [hypersonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_speed "Hypersonic speed") research with the development of the US3D [CFD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_fluid_dynamics "Computational fluid dynamics") code which builds off of NASA's DPLR code, but uses [unstructured grids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unstructured_grid "Unstructured grid") and has many advanced numerical capabilities and physical models for multi-physics, highly coupled problems.

### Greek life, professional and honor societies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Greek life, professional and honor societies")]

Main article: [University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_fraternities_and_sororities "University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities")

The University of Minnesota has numerous fraternities and sororities. Including defunct branches, the Greek system numbers more than 200 organizations, approximately half of which operate today.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-115) The university's Greek societies include the residential [academic and social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraternities_and_sororities_in_North_America "Fraternities and sororities in North America") chapters, including non-residential multicultural groups. The Greek system includes [professional fraternities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_fraternities_and_sororities "Professional fraternities and sororities"), [Hhonor Ssocieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor_society "Honor society"), Rreligious and [service Ffraternities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_fraternities_and_sororities "Service fraternities and sororities"). Fraternities and sororities have built several historically significant "Fraternity Row" homes along University Ave. SE, 10th Ave. SE, 4th Street SE, and 5th Street SE, all in Minneapolis, or along Cleveland Ave. near the St. Paul campus.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-HistoricalStudy2003-116)

As of June 2018, approximately 3,900 system members made up about 11% of the campus population. Minnesota hosts 38 academic fraternities, 20 academic sororities, 56 honors societies, 31 professional societies, and two service-focused chapters.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-OFSL2017-117)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-118)

#### Print

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Print")]

_[The Minnesota Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota\_Daily "Minnesota Daily")_ has been published twice a week during the normal school season since the fall semester 2016.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-119) It is printed weekly during the summer. The _Daily_ is operated by an autonomous organization run entirely by students. It was first published on May 1, 1900. Besides everyday news coverage, the paper has also published special issues, such as the Grapevine Awards, Ski-U-Mah, the Bar & Beer Guide, Sex-U-Mah, and others.

A long-defunct humor magazine, _[Ski-U-Mah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ski-U-Mah\_(magazine) "Ski-U-Mah (magazine)")_, was published from about 1930 to 1950. It launched the career of novelist and scriptwriter [Max Shulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Shulman "Max Shulman").

A relative newcomer to the university's print media community is _The Wake Student Magazine_, a weekly that covers UMN-related stories and provides a forum for student expression. It was founded in November 2001 in an effort to diversify campus media and achieved student group status in February 2002.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-fund-120) Students from many disciplines do all of the reporting, writing, editing, illustration, photography, layout, and business management for the publication. The magazine was founded by James DeLong and Chris Ruen.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead-121)_The Wake_ was named the nation's best campus publication (2006) by the Independent Press Association.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-fund-120)

Additionally, the _Wake_ publishes _Liminal_, a literary journal begun in 2005. _Liminal_ was created in the absence of an undergraduate literary journal and continues to bring poetry and prose to the university community.

_The Wake_ has faced a number of challenges during its existence, due in part to the reliance on student fees funding. In April 2004, after the Student Services Fees Committee had initially declined to fund it, the needed $60,000 in funding was restored, allowing the magazine to continue publishing.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead-121) It faced further challenges in 2005, when its request for additional funding to publish weekly was denied[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead2-122) and then partially restored.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead4-123)

In 2005 conservatives on campus began formulating a new publication named _The Minnesota Republic_. The first issue was released in February 2006, and funding by student service fees started in September 2006. _The Republic_ is a biweekly newspaper run entirely by students, reporting on campus, state, and national news with commentary on sports, economics, and arts and entertainment.

_The Republic_ is a member of the [Collegiate Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Network "Collegiate Network"), a program that includes over 100 publications at colleges and universities around the United States.

#### Radio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Radio")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg/500px-University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg)

The University of Minnesota on the radio version of the _[College Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College\_Bowl "College Bowl")_, c.1953–54

The campus radio station, [KUOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KUOM "KUOM") "Radio K", broadcasts an eclectic variety of [independent music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_music "Independent music") during the day on 770 [kHz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KHz "KHz")[AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AM_radio "AM radio"). Its 5,000-watt signal has a range of 80 mi (130 km), but shuts down at dusk because of [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") regulations. In 2003, the station added a low-power (8-watt) signal on 106.5 MHz [FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_radio "FM radio") overnight and on weekends. In 2005, a 10-watt translator began broadcasting from Falcon Heights on 100.7 FM at all times. Radio K also [streams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_radio "Internet radio") its content at www.radiok.org. With roots in experimental transmissions that began before World War I, the station received the first AM broadcast license in the state on January 13, 1922, and began broadcasting as [WLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_K "Radio K"), changing to the KUOM [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_call_sign "Radio call sign") about two decades later. The station had an educational format until 1993, when it merged with a smaller campus-only music station to become what is now known as Radio K. A small group of full-time employees are joined by over 20 part-time student employees who oversee the station. Most of the on-air talent consists of student volunteers.

Some television programs made on campus have been broadcast on local [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Broadcasting_Service "Public Broadcasting Service") station [KTCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTCI "KTCI") channel 17. ### Student Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Student Government")]

The Undergraduate Student Government advocates for student interests on local, state, and federal levels, and focuses on efforts that directly benefit the student population. It was instrumental in passing legislation in the 2013 Minnesota Legislature for medical amnesty.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-124)

The Council of Graduate Students and the Professional Student Government represent the interests of students in graduate and professional study programs, respectively. Formerly, they were represented by one organization known as the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly, which splintered in 2014.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-125)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-126)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Student activism")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Anti-war_protest_encampment%2C_University_of_Minnesota_in_Minneapolis_%2853694337428%29.jpg/250px-Anti-war_protest_encampment%2C_University_of_Minnesota_in_Minneapolis_%2853694337428%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anti-war_protest_encampment,_University_of_Minnesota_in_Minneapolis_(53694337428).jpg)

University of Minnesota [pro-Palestinian encampment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_pro-Palestinian_protests_on_university_campuses_in_2024 "List of pro-Palestinian protests on university campuses in 2024") on May 1, 2024

Student activism has played an important role at the university, including campaigns to desegregate campus housing in the 1930s and 1940s,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-127) Black students' take over of Morrill Hall in 1969, which led to the creation of the Department of Afro-American Studies,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-128) now known as the Department of African-American and African Studies,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-129) the 1970 student strike against war,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-130) campaigns to keep the [General College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_College_Truth_Movement "General College Truth Movement") open in the 2000s, campaigns against racism in 2014–2015 known as Whose Diversity?,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-131) and many graduate student unionization efforts. For example, labor coalition efforts in the 2021–2022 academic year highlighted poor wages, poor stipend conditions, and administrative disrespect for graduate student workers.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-132) In the 2022–2023 academic year, labor efforts materialized into a campaign and a vote that culminated in the formation of the Graduate Labor Union-United Electrical (GLU-UE), the labor union currently representing graduate student workers at the University of Minnesota.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-133)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-134)

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [Minnesota Golden Gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers "Minnesota Golden Gophers")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg/250px-Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldy_Gopher_(Bronze_and_Granite,_2015).jpg)

[Goldy Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher "Goldy Gopher") statue in front of [Coffman Memorial Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffman_Memorial_Union "Coffman Memorial Union")

Minnesota's Twin Cities campus athletics teams are called the [Minnesota Golden Gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers "Minnesota Golden Gophers") and are members of the [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference") and the [Western Collegiate Hockey Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Collegiate_Hockey_Association "Western Collegiate Hockey Association") (WCHA) in the [National Collegiate Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA). As of 2019, they have won 19 NCAA championships[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-135) and claim six national football championships.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-136)

Since the 2013–14 school year, the only Minnesota team that does not compete in the Big Ten is the [women's ice hockey team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers_women's_ice_hockey "Minnesota Golden Gophers women's ice hockey"), which competes in the WCHA. The Gophers [men's ice hockey team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers_men's_ice_hockey "Minnesota Golden Gophers men's ice hockey") was a longtime WCHA member, but left when the Big Ten began operating a [men's ice hockey league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference_(ice_hockey) "Big Ten Conference (ice hockey)") with six inaugural members. The current athletic director is [Mark Coyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Coyle "Mark Coyle").

The Golden Gophers' most notable rivalry is the annual college football game against the [Wisconsin Badgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_Badgers "Wisconsin Badgers") for [Paul Bunyan's Axe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bunyan's_Axe "Paul Bunyan's Axe"). The two universities also compete in the Border Battle, a year-long athletic competition in which each sport season is worth 40 points divided by the number of times the teams play each other (i.e. football is worth 40 points because they play each other only once, while women's ice hockey is worth 10 points per game because they play four times a year). Conference and postseason [playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playoffs "Playoffs") do not count in the point standings.

[Goldy Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher "Goldy Gopher") is the mascot for the Twin Cities campus and the associated sports teams. The [gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopher_(animal) "Gopher (animal)") mascot is a tradition as old as the state, which was tabbed the "Gopher State" in 1857 after a political cartoon ridiculing the $5 million railroad loan that helped open up the West. The cartoon portrayed shifty railroad barons as striped gophers pulling a railroad car carrying the Territorial Legislature. Later, the university picked up the nickname with the first university [yearbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook "Yearbook"), bearing the name "Gopher Annual", appearing in 1887.

The [Minnesota Rouser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Rouser "Minnesota Rouser") is the university's [fight song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_song "Fight song"). It is commonly played and sung by the 320-member [Minnesota Marching Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Marching_Band "University of Minnesota Marching Band") at events such as [commencement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduation "Graduation"), [convocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convocation "Convocation"), and athletic games. Other songs associated with the university include the [Minnesota March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_March "Minnesota March"), which was composed for the university by [John Philip Sousa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Sousa "John Philip Sousa"), and [Hail! Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail!_Minnesota "Hail! Minnesota"), the university's [alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater_(song) "Alma mater (song)") and [state song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_songs "List of U.S. state songs") of Minnesota.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-137)

The **University of Minnesota Twin Cities**[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-11) (historically known as **University of Minnesota**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[land-grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [Twin Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis%E2%80%93Saint_Paul "Minneapolis–Saint Paul") of [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") and [Saint Paul, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Saint Paul, Minnesota"), United States. It is the [flagship institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship#Colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States "Flagship") of the [University of Minnesota System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_System "University of Minnesota System") and is organized into 19 colleges, schools, and other major academic units.

Founded by the [Minnesota Territorial Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Territorial_Legislature "Minnesota Territorial Legislature") as a territorial university in 1851, seven years before Minnesota achieved statehood, the Twin Cities campus is the oldest and largest in the [University of Minnesota System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_System "University of Minnesota System"). Its enrollment of 56,666 students as of fall 2024 places it among the [ten largest U.S. campuses by enrollment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_university_campuses_by_enrollment "List of United States university campuses by enrollment").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-12) The campus comprises locations in Minneapolis and St. Paul, approximately 3 mi (4.8 km) apart.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:0-14)

The University of Minnesota is classified as an "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity" by the [Carnegie Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-15) It is a member of the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities"). The [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation") ranked the University of Minnesota 22nd among American universities for research and development expenditures in 2022 with $1.202 billion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-17)

The [Minnesota Golden Gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers "Minnesota Golden Gophers") compete in 21 intercollegiate sports in [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") as a member of the [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference") and have won 29 national championships.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-19) As of March 2024, Minnesota's current and former students have won a total of [90 Olympic medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_universities_with_Olympic_medals "List of American universities with Olympic medals"). There are 25 [Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates "List of Nobel laureates") associated with the university.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-21)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7: [icon]](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/20px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg)This section **needs expansion**. You can help by [adding missing information](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=). _(March 2020)_

The University of Minnesota was established in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis,_Minnesota "Minneapolis, Minnesota") in 1851, seven years prior to Minnesota achieving statehood, following a charter granted by the Minnesota Territorial Legislature and Governor [Alexander Ramsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ramsey "Alexander Ramsey") and the subsequent election of a board of regents.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:0-14) In its initial years, the university encountered significant challenges and depended on contributions from various donors to remain operational, notably including support from South Carolina Governor [William Aiken Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Aiken_Jr. "William Aiken Jr.").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:1-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:2-23)

In 1867, the university received land grant status through the [Morrill Act of 1862](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrill_Land-Grant_Acts "Morrill Land-Grant Acts").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-25) With lands taken from [Dakota people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people"), the university was able to revive itself after closing in 1858.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-morillgrant-26) The Dakota people have not been credited for the expropriation of their lands.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-morillgrant-26)

An 1876 donation from flour miller [John S. Pillsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Pillsbury "John S. Pillsbury") is generally credited with saving the school.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:1-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:2-23) Since then, Pillsbury has become known as "The Father of the University."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-27)[Pillsbury Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Old_Campus_Historic_District "University of Minnesota Old Campus Historic District") is named in his honor.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-29)

Academic milestones began with Warren Clark Eustis and Henry Martyn Williamson graduating in 1873 as the university's first graduates.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) Helen Marr Ely was the first female graduate in 1875.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) The university progressed by awarding its first master's degree in 1880 and conferring its first Ph.D. in 1888.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30)

As the 20th century began, the university expanded its academic offerings. In 1908, the university inaugurated the Program of Mortuary Science, becoming the first state university in the United States to do so.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) The School of Nursing was established in 1909, the first continuous nursing school on a university campus in the United States. The nursing school later opened its doors to male students in 1949.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30)

The university first integrated its faculty in 1948 when it hired its first African American, [Ruby Pernell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Pernell "Ruby Pernell").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-31)

20th-century breakthroughs at the University of Minnesota positioned it as a leader in medical innovation. In 1954, C. Walton Lillehei and F. John Lewis performed the world's first successful open-heart surgery using [cross-circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-circulation "Cross-circulation").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) 1955 saw Richard DeWall and Lillehei develop the bubble oxygenator, setting the stage for modern heart-lung machines.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) This was followed by Lillehei's performance of the first artificial heart valve implant in a human in 1958, and in the same year, Earl Bakken, co-founder of Medtronic, Inc., developed the first portable [pacemaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacemaker "Pacemaker"), introduced into practice by Lillehei.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30)

The latter part of the 20th century saw the university's continued innovation in medical transplantation, including the world's first successful kidney/pancreas transplant in 1967, a bone marrow transplant in 1968, and a living donor pancreas transplant in 1998.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30) Another notable contribution to agriculture came in 1991, with the development of the [honeycrisp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeycrisp "Honeycrisp") apple.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-UMNHistory-30)

### Minneapolis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Minneapolis")]

The original Minneapolis campus overlooked the [Saint Anthony Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Anthony_Falls "Saint Anthony Falls") on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), but it was later moved about a mile (1.6 km) downstream to its current location. The original site is now marked by a small park known as Chute Square at the intersection of University and Central avenues.

The school shut down following a financial crisis during the American Civil War, but reopened in 1867 with considerable financial help from [John S. Pillsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Pillsbury "John S. Pillsbury"). It was upgraded from a [preparatory school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University-preparatory_school "University-preparatory school") to a college in 1869. Today, the university's Minneapolis campus is divided by the Mississippi River into an East Bank and a West Bank.

The Minneapolis campus has several residence halls: 17th Avenue Hall, Centennial Hall, Frontier Hall, Territorial Hall, Pioneer Hall, Sanford Hall, Wilkins Hall, Middlebrook Hall, Yudof Hall, and Comstock Hall.

The East Bank, the main portion of the campus, covers 307 acres (124 ha) and is divided into several areas: the Knoll area, the Mall area, the Health area, the Athletic area, and the Gateway area.

The Knoll area, the oldest extant part of the university, is in the northwestern corner of the campus.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-33) Many buildings in this area are well over 100 years old, such as some of the 13 in the [Old Campus Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Old_Campus_Historic_District "University of Minnesota Old Campus Historic District").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-34) Today, most [disciplines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discipline "Discipline") in this area relate to the [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities"). Burton Hall is home to the [College of Education and Human Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Education_and_Human_Development "University of Minnesota College of Education and Human Development"). Folwell Hall and Jones Hall are primarily used by the language departments. A residence hall, Sanford Hall, and a student-apartment complex, Roy Wilkins Hall, are in this area. This area is just south of the Dinkytown neighborhood and business area.

[Northrop Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Mall_Historic_District "Northrop Mall Historic District") is arguably the center of the Minneapolis campus. The plan for the Mall was based on a design by [Cass Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_Gilbert "Cass Gilbert"), although his scheme was too extravagant to be fully implemented.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-35) Several of the campus's primary buildings surround the Mall area. [Northrop Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Auditorium "Northrop Auditorium") provides a northern anchor, with [Coffman Memorial Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffman_Memorial_Union "Coffman Memorial Union") (CMU) to the south. Four of the larger buildings to the sides of the Mall are the primary [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"), and [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry") buildings (Vincent Hall, Tate Laboratory and Smith Hall, respectively) and [Walter Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Library "Walter Library"). Smith Hall and Walter Library were built during the [Lotus Coffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotus_Coffman "Lotus Coffman") administration.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-36)

The Mall area is home to the [College of Liberal Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Liberal_Arts "University of Minnesota College of Liberal Arts"), which is Minnesota's largest public or private college, and the [College of Science and Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Institute_of_Technology "University of Minnesota Institute of Technology"). Behind CMU is another residence hall, Comstock Hall, and another student-apartment complex, Yudof Hall. The [Northrop Mall Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Mall_Historic_District "Northrop Mall Historic District") was formally listed in the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in January 2018.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-37)

The Health area is to the southeast of the Mall area and focuses on undergraduate buildings for [biological science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_science "Biological science") students, as well as the homes of the college of [Pharmacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacy "Pharmacy"), the School of [Nursing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursing "Nursing"), the [School of Dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_School_of_Dentistry "University of Minnesota School of Dentistry"), the [Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Medical_School "University of Minnesota Medical School"), the [School of Public Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_School_of_Public_Health "University of Minnesota School of Public Health"), and [M Health Fairview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M_Health_Fairview "M Health Fairview") Hospitals and Clinics. This complex of buildings forms what is known as the [University of Minnesota Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Medical_Center "University of Minnesota Medical Center"). Part of the [College of Biological Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Biological_Sciences "University of Minnesota College of Biological Sciences") is housed in this area.

Across the street from the University of Minnesota Medical Center Fairview is an area known as the "Superblock", a four-city-block space comprising four residence halls, Pioneer, Frontier, Centennial and Territorial Halls. The Superblock is one of the most popular locations for on-campus housing because it has the largest concentration of students living on campus and has a multitude of social activities between the residence halls.

The Athletic area is directly north of the Superblock and includes four recreation/athletic facilities: the University Recreation Center, Cooke Hall, the University Fieldhouse, and the [University Aquatic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Stadium_(University_of_Minnesota)#University_Aquatic_center "Memorial Stadium (University of Minnesota)"). These facilities are all connected by tunnels and skyways, allowing students to use one locker room facility. North of this complex is the [Huntington Bank Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntington_Bank_Stadium "Huntington Bank Stadium"), [Williams Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_Arena "Williams Arena"), [Mariucci Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariucci_Arena "Mariucci Arena"), [Ridder Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridder_Arena "Ridder Arena"), and the Baseline Tennis Center.

The Gateway area, the easternmost section of campus, is primarily composed of office buildings instead of classrooms and lecture halls. The most prominent building is [McNamara Alumni Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McNamara_Alumni_Center "McNamara Alumni Center"). The university is also heavily invested in a [biomedical research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomedical "Biomedical") initiative and has built five biomedical research buildings that form a biomedical complex directly north of Huntington Bank Stadium.

[The Armory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Armory "University of Minnesota Armory"), northeast of the Mall area, is built like a [Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_architecture "Norman architecture")[castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle "Castle"). It features a [sally-port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_port "Sally port") entrance facing Church Street and a tower that was originally intended to be the professor of [military science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_science "Military science")'s residence. Since it originally held the athletics department, the Armory also features a [gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gym "Gym"). Today it is home to military science classes and the university's [Reserve Officers' Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Officers'_Training_Corps "Reserve Officers' Training Corps").

Several buildings in the [Old Campus Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Old_Campus_Historic_District "University of Minnesota Old Campus Historic District") were designed by early Minnesota architect [LeRoy Buffington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leroy_Buffington "Leroy Buffington"). One of the most notable is [Pillsbury Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Old_Campus_Historic_District#Pillsbury_Hall,_1889 "University of Minnesota Old Campus Historic District"), designed by Buffington and Harvey Ellis in the [Richardsonian Romanesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardsonian_Romanesque "Richardsonian Romanesque") style. Pillsbury Hall's [polychromatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychromatic "Polychromatic") facade incorporates several sandstone varieties that were available in Minnesota during the time of construction. Buffington also designed the exterior of [Burton Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Old_Campus_Historic_District#Burton_Hall,_1894 "University of Minnesota Old Campus Historic District"), considered one of the strongest specimens of [Greek Revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Revival_architecture "Greek Revival architecture") in Minnesota.

Many of the buildings on the East Bank were designed by the prolific Minnesota architect [Clarence H. Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_H._Johnston,_Sr. "Clarence H. Johnston, Sr."), including the [Jacobean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobean_architecture "Jacobean architecture") Folwell Hall and the [Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") edifices of [Northrop Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Auditorium "Northrop Auditorium") and [Walter Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Library "Walter Library"), which he considered the heart of the university. Johnston's son, Clarence Johnston Jr, was also an architect and designed the original [Bell Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Museum_of_Natural_History "Bell Museum of Natural History") building and [Coffman Memorial Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffman_Memorial_Union "Coffman Memorial Union") in the 1930s.

The [Malcolm Moos Health Sciences Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Moos_Health_Sciences_Tower "Malcolm Moos Health Sciences Tower"), which is the tallest building on the Twin Cities campus, is a noted example of [brutalist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture").

In more recent years, [Frank Gehry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry "Frank Gehry") designed the [Frederick R. Weisman Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weisman_Art_Museum "Weisman Art Museum"). Completed in 1993, the Weisman Art Museum is a typical example of his work with curving metallic structures. The abstract structure is considered highly significant because it was built prior to the widespread use of [computer-aided design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-aided_design "Computer-aided design") in architecture. It also ushered in a new era of architecture at the university, which continued with the completion of the [McNamara Alumni Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McNamara_Alumni_Center "McNamara Alumni Center") in 2000 and Bruininks Hall (formerly STSS) in 2010.

Another notable structure is the addition to the Architecture building, designed by [Steven Holl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Holl "Steven Holl") and completed in 2002. It won an [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") award for its innovative design. The Architecture building was then renamed Rapson Hall after the local [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") architect and School of Architecture Dean [Ralph Rapson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Rapson "Ralph Rapson").

The university also has a "Greek row" of historic [fraternities and sororities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraternities_and_sororities "Fraternities and sororities") located north of campus on University Avenue SE.

Main article: [University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_fraternities_and_sororities "University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities")

### St. Paul

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: St. Paul")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/McNeal_Hall_Minnesota_5.jpg/250px-McNeal_Hall_Minnesota_5.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McNeal_Hall_Minnesota_5.jpg)

McNeal Hall houses the [Goldstein Museum of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstein_Museum_of_Design "Goldstein Museum of Design").

The St. Paul campus is by St. Paul and the suburb of [Falcon Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_Heights,_Minnesota "Falcon Heights, Minnesota"), about 3 mi (4.8 km) from the Minneapolis campus. The default place name for the ZIP code serving the campus is "St. Paul." The [College of Food, Agricultural and Natural Resource Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Food,_Agricultural_and_Natural_Resource_Sciences "University of Minnesota College of Food, Agricultural and Natural Resource Sciences"), including the University of Minnesota Food Industry Center and many other disciplines from social sciences to [vocational education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_education "Vocational education"), are on this campus. It also includes the College of Continuing and Professional Studies,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-39) College of Veterinary Medicine,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-40) and College of Biological Sciences.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-41)

The extensive lawns, flowers, trees, and surrounding University research farm plots create a greener and quieter campus. It has a grassy mall of its own and can be a bit of a retreat from the more urban Minneapolis campus. Prominent on this campus is Bailey Hall, the St. Paul campus' only residence hall. Campus Connector buses run every five minutes on weekdays when school is in session, and every 20 minutes on weekends, allowing students easy access to both campuses.

The Continuing Education and Conference Center,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-42) which serves over 20,000 conference attendees per year, is also on the St. Paul campus.

The St. Paul campus is home to the College of Design's Department of Design, Housing, and Apparel (DHA). Located in McNeal Hall, DHA includes the departmental disciplines of apparel design, graphic design, housing studies, interior design, and retail merchandising. McNeal Hall, named for [Wylle B. McNeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wylle_B._McNeal "Wylle B. McNeal"), the third head of home economics at Minnesota, is also the home to the university's [Goldstein Museum of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldstein_Museum_of_Design "Goldstein Museum of Design").

The St. Paul campus is known to University students and staff for the Meat and Dairy Salesroom,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-43) which sells animal food products (such as ice cream, cheese, and meat) produced in the university's state-certified pilot plant by students, faculty and staff.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-44)

The St. Paul campus borders the [Minnesota State Fairgrounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_State_Fair "Minnesota State Fair"), which hosts the largest [state fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_fair "State fair") in the United States by daily attendance.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-45) The fair lasts 12 days, from late August through Labor Day. The grounds also serve a variety of functions during the rest of the year.

Although the Falcon Heights [area code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Numbering_Plan "North American Numbering Plan") is 651, the university telephone system trunk lines use Minneapolis [exchanges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone_exchange "Telephone exchange") and its 612 area code.

### Commuting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Commuting")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Washington_Ave_Bridge.jpg/250px-Washington_Ave_Bridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_Ave_Bridge.jpg)

The [Washington Avenue Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Avenue_Bridge_(Minneapolis) "Washington Avenue Bridge (Minneapolis)") connects the East Bank and West Bank portions of the [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") campus.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Green_Line%2C_Coffman_Union%2C_and_bus_stop.jpg/250px-Green_Line%2C_Coffman_Union%2C_and_bus_stop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Line,_Coffman_Union,_and_bus_stop.jpg)

A [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Minnesota) "Green Line (Minnesota)") train after leaving the [East Bank Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bank_(Metro_Transit_station) "East Bank (Metro Transit station)"), heading towards [Downtown Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Minneapolis "Downtown Minneapolis")

Walking and riding bicycles are the most common modes of transportation among students. At times, the University Police has occasionally cited individuals for [jaywalking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaywalking "Jaywalking") or riding bicycles on restricted sidewalks in areas surrounding the university.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-46)

The [Washington Avenue Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Avenue_Bridge_(Minneapolis) "Washington Avenue Bridge (Minneapolis)") crossing the Mississippi River provides access between the East and West Banks in Minneapolis, on foot and via designated bike lanes and a free shuttle service. Several pedestrian tunnels ease the passage from building to building during harsh weather; they are marked with signs reading "[The Gopher Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gopher_Way "The Gopher Way")". The Minneapolis campus is near [Interstates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System")[94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94 "Interstate 94") and [35W](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_35 "Interstate 35") and is bordered by the Minneapolis neighborhoods of [Dinkytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinkytown "Dinkytown") (on the north), [Cedar-Riverside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar-Riverside,_Minneapolis "Cedar-Riverside, Minneapolis") (on the west), [Stadium Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_Village "Stadium Village") (on the southeast), and [Prospect Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospect_Park,_Minneapolis "Prospect Park, Minneapolis") (on the east).

On regular weekdays during the school year, the Campus Connectors operate with schedule-less service as often as every five minutes during the busiest parts of the school day (between 7 am and 5:30 pm), slowing to once every 15 or 20 minutes during earlier or later hours.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-47) The estimated commute time between St. Paul and the East Bank is 15 minutes.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-48)

In 2008, the system carried 3.55 million riders. Although the shuttle service is free, it is comparatively inexpensive to operate; with an operating cost of $4.55 million in 2008, the operating subsidy was only $1.28 per passenger. Even [Metro Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Transit_(Minnesota) "Metro Transit (Minnesota)")'s busy [Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_(Minnesota) "Metro (Minnesota)")[Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(Minnesota) "Blue Line (Minnesota)") light rail required a subsidy of $1.44 that year, and that was with many riders paying $1.75 or more for a ride.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-49)

Three [light-rail stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail_in_Minnesota "Light rail in Minnesota") serve the university along the [Green Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Line_(Minnesota) "Green Line (Minnesota)"): [Stadium Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_Village_(Metro_Transit_station) "Stadium Village (Metro Transit station)"), [East Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bank_(Metro_Transit_station) "East Bank (Metro Transit station)"), and [West Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bank_(Metro_Transit_station) "West Bank (Metro Transit station)"). The university partnered with [Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_(Minnesota) "Metro (Minnesota)") to offer students, staff, and faculty members a [Campus Zone Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go-To_card#Campus_Zone_Pass "Go-To card") that enables free travel on the three stations that pass through campus,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-50) as well as a discounted unlimited pass for students.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-51) More recently, the university has instituted the Universal Transit Pass, which allows most students unlimited access to the Metro Transit light rail and bus networks as well as a number of other transit systems in the area.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-52)

### Campus safety

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Campus safety")]

The Step Up campaign is a program that helps students prevent excessive drinking, as well as sexual assault and other crimes, by teaching them how to intervene and prevent in a positive way.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Step_Up-53) This is done, in part, by explaining the [bystander effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bystander_effect "Bystander effect"). The U of M also has a SAFE-U emergency notification text messaging system that sends out a notification to all faculty, staff, and students in case of emergency.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-TXT_-_U-54) The commitment to a safe inclusive campus is also articulated through the comprehensive University of Minnesota Safety Plan, aligned with MPact 2025's Commitment 5, Action Item 5.4, emphasizing the need to assess and improve campus safety continually.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:4-55)

The establishment of the Strategic Safety Advisory Committee and public safety forums fosters community engagement and dialogue on safety concerns and improvements. The university has made strides in off-campus safety through nightly patrols in Dinkytown and the introduction of blue light kiosks and mobile light trailers to enhance visibility and security. Other resources help students get home safely. Calling 624-WALK secures an escort for walks to adjacent campuses and neighborhoods, and Gopher Chauffeur, a van service, offers rides near and on campus. Both are free and open to all students, staff, and faculty.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Creating_a_safe_U-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-60)

The campus has nearly 200 automated external defibrillators (AEDs) and 200 yellow phones for emergency-only calls. The University Police Station has 20 Code Blue phones around campus that immediately connect people to their office. There are over 2,000 security cameras being monitored 24 hours a day.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Creating_a_safe_U-56) The university maintains a vigilant stance on cybersecurity, conducting annual external assessments and updating strategies for risk mitigation. Emergency preparedness is a key focus, with updated Emergency Operations Plans and disaster recovery protocols ensuring readiness for a variety of potential threats.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:4-55)

#### Sexual assaults

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sexual assaults")]

Minnesota Gophers football player [Dominic Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Jones "Dominic Jones") was convicted of sexual assault in 2008.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-61) In July 2009, an appeals court upheld Jones' conviction, but reduced his four-year prison sentence to one year.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-sentence-62) More than 1,000 sexual assaults on campus were reported between 2010 and 2015.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Tribune-63) No prosecutions for rape occurred, according to Katie Eichele of the Aurora Center,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Tribune-63) until the conviction of [Daniel Drill-Mellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_University_of_Minnesota_rape_case "2014 University of Minnesota rape case") in 2016, for the rapes of two fellow students.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-2016conviction-64) Drill-Mellum received a six-year prison sentence.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-2016conviction-64)

It has been alleged that few sexual assaults on campus are reported to University police.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Fox9-65) Six resulted in arrest from 2010 to 2015; one was determined to be unfounded.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Fox9-65) In a study by campus police, in the years between 2005 and 2015, sexual assaults at the university remained the same or increased[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-66) despite six sexual assault resources and many anti-crime programs on campus.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-70) In August 2020, the University of Minnesota agreed to pay $500,000 to a woman who in the fall of 2016, accused several Gophers football players of sexually assaulting her.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-71) In February 2017, a University of Minnesota panel cleared four of the 10 Gopher football players the woman accused and agreed with investigators' recommendation that four other players be expelled and the other two players should be suspended for a year.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-72)
