In 2024, Minnesota was ranked as the 26th best university in the United States by the _[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic\_Ranking\_of\_World\_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")_, and 25th in the United States in _[Washington Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Monthly "Washington Monthly")_'s 2021 National University Rankings.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-95) Minnesota's undergraduate program was ranked 53rd among national universities by _[U.S. News & World Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_News\_&\_World\_Report "U.S. News & World Report")_ for 2023, and 23rd in the nation among public colleges and universities.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-96) The same publication ranked Minnesota's graduate [Carlson School of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlson_School_of_Management "Carlson School of Management") as 28th in the nation among business schools, and 6th in the nation for its information systems graduate program.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-auto-97) Other graduate schools ranked highly by _U.S. News & World Report_ for 2022 include the [University of Minnesota Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Law_School "University of Minnesota Law School") at 22nd, the [University of Minnesota Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Medical_School "University of Minnesota Medical School"), which was 4th for family medicine and 5th for primary care, the [University of Minnesota College of Pharmacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Pharmacy "University of Minnesota College of Pharmacy"), which ranked 3rd, the [Hubert H. Humphrey School of Public Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_H._Humphrey_School_of_Public_Affairs "Hubert H. Humphrey School of Public Affairs"), which ranked 9th, the [University of Minnesota College of Education and Human Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_College_of_Education_and_Human_Development "University of Minnesota College of Education and Human Development"), which ranked 10th for education psychology and special education, and the [University of Minnesota School of Public Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_School_of_Public_Health "University of Minnesota School of Public Health"), which ranked 10th.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-auto-97)

In 2020, the [Center for Measuring University Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Measuring_University_Performance "Center for Measuring University Performance") ranked Minnesota 16th in the nation in terms of total research, 30th in endowment assets, 24th in annual giving, 28th in the number of [National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academies_of_Sciences,_Engineering_and_Medicine "National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine") memberships, 9th in its number of faculty awards, and 14th in its number of [National Merit Scholars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Merit_Scholars "National Merit Scholars").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-98) Minnesota is listed as a "[Public Ivy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Ivy "Public Ivy")" in 2001 Greenes' Guides _The Public Ivies: America's Flagship Public Universities_.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-99)

In 2021, the University of Minnesota was ranked as the 40th best university in the world by the _[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic\_Ranking\_of\_World\_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities") (ARWU)_, which assesses academic and research performance.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:3-100) The same 2021 ranking by subject placed the University of Minnesota's ecology program as 2nd best in the world, management program as 10th best, biotechnology program as 11th best, mechanical engineering and medical technology programs as 14th best, law and psychology programs as 19th best, and veterinary sciences program as 20th best.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-:3-100) The Center for World University Rankings (CWUR) for 2021–22 ranked Minnesota 46th in the world and 26th in the United States.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-101) The 2021 Nature Index, which assesses the institutions that dominate high-quality research output, ranked Minnesota 53rd in the world based on research publication data from 2020.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-102)_[U.S. News & World Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_News\_&\_World\_Report "U.S. News & World Report")_ ranked Minnesota as the 47th best global university for 2021.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-103) The 2015 _[Times Higher Education World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times\_Higher\_Education\_World\_University\_Rankings "Times Higher Education World University Rankings")_ placed Minnesota 46th worldwide, based primarily on teaching, research, knowledge transfer, and international outlook.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-104)

## Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Research")]

Inventions by University of Minnesota students and faculty have ranged from food science to health technologies. Most of the public research funding in Minnesota is funneled to the University of Minnesota as a result of long-standing advocacy by the university itself.

The university developed [Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopher_(protocol) "Gopher (protocol)"),[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-105) a precursor to the [World Wide Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web") which used [hyperlinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlinks "Hyperlinks") to connect documents across computers on the internet. However, the version produced by [CERN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN") was favored by the public since it was freely distributed and could more easily handle multimedia webpages.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-106) The university also houses the [Charles Babbage Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Babbage_Institute "Charles Babbage Institute"), a research and archive center specializing in computer history. The department has strong roots in the early days of supercomputing with [Seymour Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Cray "Seymour Cray") of [Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cray "Cray") supercomputers.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-107)

The university also became a member of the [Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Interferometer_Gravitational-wave_Observatory "Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory") (LIGO) in 2007 and has led data analysis projects searching for gravitational waves — their existence [was confirmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_observation_of_gravitational_waves "First observation of gravitational waves") by scientists in February 2016.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-timeshighereducation.com-32)

Discoveries and innovation by faculty or alumni include:

*   [Puffed rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puffed_rice "Puffed rice") – [Alexander P. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_P._Anderson "Alexander P. Anderson") performed work leading to the discovery of "puffed rice", a starting point for a new breakfast cereal later advertised as "Food Shot From Guns".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-108)
*   Transistorized cardiac pacemaker – [Earl Bakken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Bakken "Earl Bakken") founded Medtronic, where he developed the first external, battery-operated, transistorized, wearable artificial pacemaker in 1957.
*   [Green Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution "Green Revolution") – [Norman Borlaug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Borlaug "Norman Borlaug") was an agronomist who led initiatives worldwide that contributed to extensive increases in agricultural production termed the Green Revolution. Borlaug, often called "the father of the Green Revolution", is credited with saving over a billion people worldwide from starvation. Borlaug was awarded multiple honors for his work, including the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom"), and the [Congressional Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Gold_Medal "Congressional Gold Medal").
*   [ATP synthase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATP_synthase "ATP synthase") – [Paul D. Boyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_D._Boyer "Paul D. Boyer") elucidated the enzymatic mechanism for synthesis of the cellular "energy currency", [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") (ATP), leading to a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1997.
*   [Point-contact transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-contact_transistor "Point-contact transistor") – [Walter Houser Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Houser_Brattain "Walter Houser Brattain") and [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen"), later joined by [William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley "William Shockley"), invented the point-contact transistor in December 1947. For their invention, the trio was awarded a [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") in 1956.
*   [Infusion pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infusion_pump "Infusion pump") – [Henry Buchwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Buchwald "Henry Buchwald") invented the world's first infusion port, peritoneovenous shunts, and specialty vascular catheters. He also invented the first implantable infusion pump, a precursor to implantable infusion pumps in use throughout the world today.
*   [Photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis") – [Melvin Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Calvin "Melvin Calvin") discovered the [Calvin cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_cycle "Calvin cycle") along with Andrew Benson and James Bassham; for this, he won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
*   [Ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecology "Ecology") – [Raymond Lindeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Lindeman "Raymond Lindeman") revolutionized ecology, primarily through his 1942 paper "Trophic Dynamic Aspect of Ecology", which described how energy and nutrients cycled through ecosystems.
*   [Supercomputer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer") – [Seymour Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Cray "Seymour Cray") designed a series of computers that were the fastest in the world for decades, and founded Cray Research, which built many of these machines.
*   [Taconite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taconite "Taconite") – [Edward Wilson Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Wilson_Davis "Edward Wilson Davis") developed an engineering process to economically extract iron ore from hard taconite rocks, making taconite valuable as iron ore for the iron and steel industries.
*   [Cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays "Cosmic rays") – [Phyllis S. Freier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllis_S._Freier "Phyllis S. Freier") discovered the presence of heavy nuclei in cosmic rays, proving the similarity between the Solar System and the rest of the galaxy.
*   U.S. aviation – [Robert Rowe Gilruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rowe_Gilruth "Robert Rowe Gilruth") led the development of flying qualities for airplanes, the use of rockets to achieve data at supersonic speeds, and the establishment of many of the nation's leading flight research and human space flight operations facilities.
*   [Bone marrow transplant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_marrow_transplant "Bone marrow transplant") – [Robert A. Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Good "Robert A. Good") in 1968 performed the first successful human bone marrow transplant between persons who were not identical twins and is regarded as a founder of modern immunology. In 2018 Minnesota Gov. [Mark Dayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dayton "Mark Dayton") proclaimed August 24 as University of Minnesota Blood and Marrow Transplant Day.
*   [Gore-Tex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gore-Tex "Gore-Tex") – [Robert Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_W._Gore "Robert W. Gore") invented Gore-Tex materials in 1969.
*   [Disk drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_drive "Disk drive") – [Reynold B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynold_B._Johnson "Reynold B. Johnson") invented a method and machinery to score tests electronically.
*   [K-rations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-rations "K-rations") – [Ancel Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancel_Keys "Ancel Keys") developed the rations for the U.S. military and also conducted dietary studies: the Minnesota Starvation Study and the Seven Countries Study.
*   [Synthetic rubber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_rubber "Synthetic rubber") – [Izaak Kolthoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izaak_Kolthoff "Izaak Kolthoff") developed the "cold process" for producing synthetic rubber, which he undertook under the U.S. synthetic rubber program during World War II.
*   [Cyclotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotron "Cyclotron") – [Ernest Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lawrence "Ernest Lawrence") won the Nobel Prize for Physics 1939 for inventing and developing the cyclotron.
*   _[Drosophila melanogaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila\_melanogaster "Drosophila melanogaster")_ – [Edward Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_B._Lewis "Edward B. Lewis") won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995 for his work on the _Drosophila_ bithorax complex of homeotic genes.
*   [Cardiac surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiac_surgery "Cardiac surgery") – [C. Walton Lillehei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Walton_Lillehei "C. Walton Lillehei") pioneered open-heart surgery, as well as numerous techniques, equipment, and prostheses for cardiothoracic surgery.
*   [POPmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/POPmail "POPmail") – [Mark P. McCahill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_P._McCahill "Mark P. McCahill") led the development of the Gopher protocol, the effective predecessor of the World Wide Web; was involved in creating and codifying the standard for Uniform Resource Locators (URLs); and led the development of POPmail, one of the first e-mail clients, which had a foundational influence on later e-mail clients and the popularization of graphical user interfaces in Internet technologies more broadly.
*   [MMPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Multiphasic_Personality_Inventory "Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory") – [Starke R. Hathaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starke_R._Hathaway "Starke R. Hathaway") and [J. C. McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._McKinley "J. C. McKinley") created the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), which was first published in 1943.
*   [Zatocoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zatocoding "Zatocoding") – [Calvin Mooers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Mooers "Calvin Mooers") developed a mechanical system using superimposed codes of descriptors for information retrieval called Zatocoding, 1948.
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Edward P. Ney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_P._Ney "Edward P. Ney") discovered cosmic ray heavy nuclei and solar proton events. After early work involving separating isotopes from uranium, he worked on the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project").
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Alfred O. C. Nier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_O._C._Nier "Alfred O. C. Nier") devised a method to isolate the isotopes of uranium, a critical discovery in the atomic age. Nier worked with [Kellex Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellex_Corporation "Kellex Corporation") in New York City on the design and development of efficient and effective mass spectrographs for use in the Manhattan Project to build the atomic bomb in World War II. He designed most of the spectrographs used for monitoring uranium separations during the war.
*   [Atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") – [Frank Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Oppenheimer "Frank Oppenheimer") worked on uranium isotope separation in 1945 and joined the Manhattan Project.
*   [Biotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology "Biotechnology") – [Ronald L. Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_L._Phillips "Ronald L. Phillips") was the first to generate whole corn plants from cells grown in culture, which laid the foundation for, and sparked, a new industry using cell-culture methods to genetically modify corn plants and other cereals. The corn cell line most widely used for genetic modification of corn has greatly accelerated the improvement of corn as food, feed, and fuel.
*   [Renewable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") – [Lanny D. Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanny_D._Schmidt "Lanny D. Schmidt") designed a reactor to extract hydrogen from ethanol, offering the first real hope hydrogen could be a source of inexpensive and renewable energy.
*   [Biomimetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomimetics "Biomimetics") – [Otto Schmitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Schmitt "Otto Schmitt") invented the Schmitt trigger, the cathode follower, the differential amplifier, and the chopper-stabilized amplifier.
*   [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") – [Deke Slayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deke_Slayton "Deke Slayton") was one of the original NASA Mercury Seven astronauts and became NASA's first chief of the Astronaut Office. He served as NASA's director of flight crew operations, making him responsible for crew assignments at NASA, from November 1963 until March 1972. At that time, he was granted medical clearance to fly and was assigned as the docking module pilot of the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, at age 51 becoming the oldest person to fly in space at the time.
*   [Bathythermograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathythermograph "Bathythermograph") – [Athelstan Spilhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athelstan_Spilhaus "Athelstan Spilhaus") fully developed the bathythermograph (BT) in 1938, an instrument he perfected that was of vital importance in World War II against the German U-boat. During the war, the BT became standard equipment on all U.S. Navy subs and vessels involved in antisubmarine warfare.
*   [CDC 6600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDC_6600 "CDC 6600") – [James Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_E._Thornton "James E. Thornton") developed the CDC 6600, the world's first supercomputer, designed with Seymour Cray.
*   [Ziagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziagen "Ziagen") – [Robert Vince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Vince_(scientist) "Robert Vince (scientist)") worked on antiviral drug candidates at UMN, where he went on to develop carbocyclic nucleosides termed 'carbovirs.' This class of medicinal agents included the drug abacavir. Abacavir was commercialized by GlaxoSmithKline as Ziagen for the treatment of AIDS.
*   US3D[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-109) – Graham Candler[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-110) pioneered the future of [hypersonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_speed "Hypersonic speed") research with the development of the US3D [CFD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_fluid_dynamics "Computational fluid dynamics") code which builds off of NASA's DPLR code, but uses [unstructured grids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unstructured_grid "Unstructured grid") and has many advanced numerical capabilities and physical models for multi-physics, highly coupled problems.

### Greek life, professional and honor societies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Greek life, professional and honor societies")]

Main article: [University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_fraternities_and_sororities "University of Minnesota fraternities and sororities")

The University of Minnesota has numerous fraternities and sororities. Including defunct branches, the Greek system numbers more than 200 organizations, approximately half of which operate today.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-115) The university's Greek societies include the residential [academic and social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraternities_and_sororities_in_North_America "Fraternities and sororities in North America") chapters, including non-residential multicultural groups. The Greek system includes [professional fraternities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_fraternities_and_sororities "Professional fraternities and sororities"), [Hhonor Ssocieties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor_society "Honor society"), Rreligious and [service Ffraternities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_fraternities_and_sororities "Service fraternities and sororities"). Fraternities and sororities have built several historically significant "Fraternity Row" homes along University Ave. SE, 10th Ave. SE, 4th Street SE, and 5th Street SE, all in Minneapolis, or along Cleveland Ave. near the St. Paul campus.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-HistoricalStudy2003-116)

As of June 2018, approximately 3,900 system members made up about 11% of the campus population. Minnesota hosts 38 academic fraternities, 20 academic sororities, 56 honors societies, 31 professional societies, and two service-focused chapters.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-OFSL2017-117)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-118)

#### Print

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Print")]

_[The Minnesota Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota\_Daily "Minnesota Daily")_ has been published twice a week during the normal school season since the fall semester 2016.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-119) It is printed weekly during the summer. The _Daily_ is operated by an autonomous organization run entirely by students. It was first published on May 1, 1900. Besides everyday news coverage, the paper has also published special issues, such as the Grapevine Awards, Ski-U-Mah, the Bar & Beer Guide, Sex-U-Mah, and others.

A long-defunct humor magazine, _[Ski-U-Mah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ski-U-Mah\_(magazine) "Ski-U-Mah (magazine)")_, was published from about 1930 to 1950. It launched the career of novelist and scriptwriter [Max Shulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Shulman "Max Shulman").

A relative newcomer to the university's print media community is _The Wake Student Magazine_, a weekly that covers UMN-related stories and provides a forum for student expression. It was founded in November 2001 in an effort to diversify campus media and achieved student group status in February 2002.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-fund-120) Students from many disciplines do all of the reporting, writing, editing, illustration, photography, layout, and business management for the publication. The magazine was founded by James DeLong and Chris Ruen.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead-121)_The Wake_ was named the nation's best campus publication (2006) by the Independent Press Association.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-fund-120)

Additionally, the _Wake_ publishes _Liminal_, a literary journal begun in 2005. _Liminal_ was created in the absence of an undergraduate literary journal and continues to bring poetry and prose to the university community.

_The Wake_ has faced a number of challenges during its existence, due in part to the reliance on student fees funding. In April 2004, after the Student Services Fees Committee had initially declined to fund it, the needed $60,000 in funding was restored, allowing the magazine to continue publishing.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead-121) It faced further challenges in 2005, when its request for additional funding to publish weekly was denied[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead2-122) and then partially restored.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-dead4-123)

In 2005 conservatives on campus began formulating a new publication named _The Minnesota Republic_. The first issue was released in February 2006, and funding by student service fees started in September 2006. _The Republic_ is a biweekly newspaper run entirely by students, reporting on campus, state, and national news with commentary on sports, economics, and arts and entertainment.

_The Republic_ is a member of the [Collegiate Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Network "Collegiate Network"), a program that includes over 100 publications at colleges and universities around the United States.

#### Radio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Radio")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg/500px-University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Minnesota_on_College_Bowl_1953-54.jpg)

The University of Minnesota on the radio version of the _[College Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College\_Bowl "College Bowl")_, c.1953–54

The campus radio station, [KUOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KUOM "KUOM") "Radio K", broadcasts an eclectic variety of [independent music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_music "Independent music") during the day on 770 [kHz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KHz "KHz")[AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AM_radio "AM radio"). Its 5,000-watt signal has a range of 80 mi (130 km), but shuts down at dusk because of [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") regulations. In 2003, the station added a low-power (8-watt) signal on 106.5 MHz [FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_radio "FM radio") overnight and on weekends. In 2005, a 10-watt translator began broadcasting from Falcon Heights on 100.7 FM at all times. Radio K also [streams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_radio "Internet radio") its content at www.radiok.org. With roots in experimental transmissions that began before World War I, the station received the first AM broadcast license in the state on January 13, 1922, and began broadcasting as [WLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_K "Radio K"), changing to the KUOM [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_call_sign "Radio call sign") about two decades later. The station had an educational format until 1993, when it merged with a smaller campus-only music station to become what is now known as Radio K. A small group of full-time employees are joined by over 20 part-time student employees who oversee the station. Most of the on-air talent consists of student volunteers.

Some television programs made on campus have been broadcast on local [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Broadcasting_Service "Public Broadcasting Service") station [KTCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTCI "KTCI") channel 17. Several episodes of _Great Conversations_ have been made since 2002, featuring one-on-one discussions between University faculty and experts brought in from around the world. _Tech Talk_ was a show meant to help people who feel intimidated by modern technology, including cell phones and computers.

The Undergraduate Student Government advocates for student interests on local, state, and federal levels, and focuses on efforts that directly benefit the student population. It was instrumental in passing legislation in the 2013 Minnesota Legislature for medical amnesty.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-124)

The Council of Graduate Students and the Professional Student Government represent the interests of students in graduate and professional study programs, respectively. Formerly, they were represented by one organization known as the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly, which splintered in 2014.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-125)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-126)

Student activism has played an important role at the university, including campaigns to desegregate campus housing in the 1930s and 1940s,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-127) Black students' take over of Morrill Hall in 1969, which led to the creation of the Department of Afro-American Studies,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-128) now known as the Department of African-American and African Studies,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-129) the 1970 student strike against war,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-130) campaigns to keep the [General College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_College_Truth_Movement "General College Truth Movement") open in the 2000s, campaigns against racism in 2014–2015 known as Whose Diversity?,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota#cite_note-131) and many graduate student unionization efforts. The Golden Gophers' most notable rivalry is the annual college football game against the [Wisconsin Badgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_Badgers "Wisconsin Badgers") for [Paul Bunyan's Axe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bunyan's_Axe "Paul Bunyan's Axe"). The two universities also compete in the Border Battle, a year-long athletic competition in which each sport season is worth 40 points divided by the number of times the teams play each other (i.e. football is worth 40 points because they play each other only once, while women's ice hockey is worth 10 points per game because they play four times a year). Conference and postseason [playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playoffs "Playoffs") do not count in the point standings.

[Goldy Gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher "Goldy Gopher") is the mascot for the Twin Cities campus and the associated sports teams. The [gopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopher_(animal) "Gopher (animal)") mascot is a tradition as old as the state, which was tabbed the "Gopher State" in 1857 after a political cartoon ridiculing the $5 million railroad loan that helped open up the West. The cartoon portrayed shifty railroad barons as striped gophers pulling a railroad car carrying the Territorial Legislature. Later, the university picked up the nickname with the first university [yearbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook "Yearbook"), bearing the name "Gopher Annual", appearing in 1887.

The [Minnesota Rouser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Rouser "Minnesota Rouser") is the university's [fight song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_song "Fight song"). From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Mascot of Yale University's sports teams

**Handsome Dan** is a [bulldog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulldog "Bulldog") that serves as the [mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot "Mascot") of [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")'s sports teams. In addition to a person wearing a [costume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume "Costume"), the position is filled by an actual bulldog, the honor and title being transferred to a successor upon death or retirement.

## Handsome Dan I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Handsome Dan I")]

Active 1889–1897 (retired to England).

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale%27s_mascot.jpg/250px-Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale%27s_mascot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale's_mascot.jpg)

The original Handsome Dan, bought by [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") tackle Andrew Graves in 1889

Handsome Dan was selected based on his ability to tolerate bands and children, negative reaction to the color [crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimson "Crimson") and to [tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigers "Tigers") (the symbols of rival schools [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard "Harvard") and [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") respectively), bought by Yale student Andrew Barbey Graves,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) who cleaned up the dog and named him “Handsome Dan.” Soon, Dan followed Graves everywhere around campus, including sporting events.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The students quickly adopted Dan as the Yale mascot. After Graves graduated and returned to England, Dan stayed on campus with his master's brother, William Leon Graves.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) Before football and baseball games would begin, Handsome Dan founded a tradition and a dynasty by being led across the field. One newspaper reported: "He was a big white bulldog, with one of the greatest faces a dog of that breed (English) ever carried". This was not an exaggeration, as Handsome Dan was one of the finest specimens of his breed in America, and went on to win first prize at the [Westminster Dog Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Dog_Show "Westminster Dog Show") and at least thirty other first prize ribbons in the United States and Canada.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tim_Cohane_pp._72-73-4) According to the [Hartford Courant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford_Courant "Hartford Courant"), "In personal appearance, he seemed like a cross between an alligator and a horned frog, and he was called handsome by the metaphysicians under the law of compensation. The title came to him, he never sought it. He was always taken to games on a leash, and the Harvard football team for years owed its continued existence to the fact that the rope held."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The Philadelphia Press reported that "a favorite trick was to tell him to 'Speak to Harvard.' He would bark ferociously and work himself into physical contortions of rage never before dreamed of by a dog. Dan was peculiar to himself in one thing – he would never associate with anyone but students. Dan implanted himself more firmly in the hearts of Yale students than any mascot had ever done before."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) Handsome Dan crossed the Atlantic to join his old master in 1897 and died in 1898. Graves had Dan [taxidermied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxidermy "Taxidermy") and returned him to be displayed at Yale in the old gymnasium. When it was torn down, Dan I was sent to the [Peabody Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History "Peabody Museum of Natural History") for reconstruction. Handsome Dan I now is in a sealed glass case in one of the trophy rooms of Yale's [Payne Whitney Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payne_Whitney_Gymnasium "Payne Whitney Gymnasium"), where, according to Stanton Ford, "he is the perpetual guardian of the treasures which attest to generations of Yale athletic glory." Andrew Graves died of [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") on February 18, 1948, in Westbury, Long Island.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-5)

## Handsome Dan II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Handsome Dan II")]

Active 1933–1937 (died of a broken leg).  
 After a 35-year interval, Handsome Dan II was purchased with pennies donated by the freshman class, and given to [coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(sport) "Coach (sport)")[Ducky Pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ducky_Pond "Ducky Pond").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) Handsome Dan II was [dognapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dognapping "Dognapping") by Harvard students the day before the 1934 [Harvard-Yale football game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard-Yale_football_games_(The_Game) "Harvard-Yale football games (The Game)"), and Yale students were alarmed at photographs of him happily seated at the foot of the statue of [John Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvard_(clergyman) "John Harvard (clergyman)") in [Harvard Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard "Harvard Yard"), having a snack.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) He died of a leg fracture received from a jump. Handsome Dan II is now located at the Yale Peabody Museum.

## Handsome Dan III

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Handsome Dan III")]

Active 1937–1938 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Handsome Dan III was a huge white dog who exhibited morbid [fear of crowds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoraphobia "Agoraphobia") and had to be retired.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIII-7)

## Handsome Dan IV

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Handsome Dan IV")]

Active 1938–1940 (retired due to injury).  
 Handsome Dan IV had his spine fractured by a car early in his term of office, leaving his hind legs paralyzed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8) Until he eventually died in 1940, a bulldog named Bull served in his place, becoming Handsome Dan V.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8)

## Handsome Dan V

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Handsome Dan V")]

Active 1940–1947 (died of old age).  
 "Bull", brought in his youth to watch football practices by his owner, high school student Bob Day, who lived near the [Yale Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Bowl "Yale Bowl"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanV-9) ascended to office when Handsome Dan IV died.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8) A great success, he loved public appearances and the adulation of crowds, was a familiar figure around the [locker rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locker_room "Locker room"), and joined the team on a trip to [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanV-9)

## Handsome Dan VI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VI")]

Active 1947–1949 (died at age two).  
 Handsome Dan VI was eight weeks old when he took the role, but died at age two.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVI-10) It was reported that he died from fear of [fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks") at the Yale-Harvard game, or of shame from seeing the Yale team lose to both Princeton and Harvard in the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVI-10)

## Handsome Dan VII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VII")]

Active 1949–1952 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Handsome Dan VII was donated to football coach [Herman Hickman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Hickman "Herman Hickman") at age 3 but he proved to have a bad temper, which suited him better in his next position as a watchdog on a [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") estate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVII-11)

## Handsome Dan VIII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VIII")]

Active 1952 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Up to this point, Handsome Dans had lived at the Yale Boathouse and were cared for in a somewhat haphazard fashion. Handsome Dan VIII, however, was owned by assistant football manager Tom Shutt,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVIII-12) ushering in a new era of family membership for the office-holder. Nevertheless, he had to retire after only two games due to intense discomfort with public appearances.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVIII-12)

## Handsome Dan IX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Handsome Dan IX")]

Active 1953–1959 (died of acute [kidney disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_disease "Kidney disease")).  
 Notable for falling off the dock at the Yale Boathouse and nearly drowning[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) (confirming the hypothesis that bulldogs cannot swim, due to the peculiarities of their physiques); some contemporary news reports say that he had to be [resuscitated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resuscitate "Resuscitate") after having had his head embedded in the mud.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) He also appeared on the cover of _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ magazine in November, 1956. "Danny" was born September 11, 1953, and owned by John E. Sanders, Assistant Professor of Geology, after an earlier custody by physical education instructor Alfred E. Scholz and Varsity Crew Coach Jim Rothschmidt.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) He made his mascot debut at the age of six weeks and an [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") at his death revealed that he succumbed to acute [nephrotic syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nephrotic_syndrome "Nephrotic syndrome").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13)

## Handsome Dan X

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Handsome Dan X")]

Active 1959–1969 (retired due to old age).  
 "Woodie" _aka_ "Boodnick", also owned by John E. Sanders, marked a return to the high standards seen in Handsome Dan V. An impressive 74 pounds, a beloved family pet as well as winner of the best bulldog title at the [Cape Cod Kennel Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Kennel_Club?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cape Cod Kennel Club (page does not exist)")[conformation dog show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformation_dog_show "Conformation dog show"), he was instrumental in leading Yale's football team to its 9 and 0 season in 1960. He spent several years commuting to New Haven, CT, from Dobbs Ferry, NY, prior to his retirement. His registered AKC kennel name was "Bayside Woodnought." He was sired by Ch. Bonny Boy of Fearnought out of Woodside's Christie Lou, and was a grandson of the famed Kippax Fearnought, the celebrated English import, who went Best in Show in 1955 at Westminster. He died in 1971 of natural causes.

## Handsome Dan XI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XI")]

Active 1969–1974 (retired due to [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis")).  
 "Oliver", owned by Yale's Pierson College master [John Hersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hersey "John Hersey"), loved football but had a tendency to doze in the sun during games. He was frequently sighted on [Martha's Vineyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha's_Vineyard "Martha's Vineyard") during the tourist season.

## Handsome Dan XII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XII")]

Active 1975–1984.  
 "Bingo", owned by history professor [Rollin G. Osterweis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rollin_G._Osterweis "Rollin G. Osterweis"), was described by her owner as "pugnacious and stubborn, but lovable."[_[quote needs citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Inline\_citation#When\_you\_must\_use\_inline\_citations "Wikipedia:Inline citation")_] Bingo also had the distinction of being the only female Handsome Dan. Bingo was stolen by four Princeton undergrads posing as Yale cheerleaders. They took Bingo to a friend's apartment in New York City on the run from authorities. The mastermind behind the canine-caper was Rod Shepard. The group of students took Bingo back to her owner and held a press conference for her return.

## Handsome Dan XIII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XIII")]

Active 1984–1995; 1996 (retired due to old age).  
He was also known as "Maurice" and was owned by Chris Getman, Yale Class of 1964.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:1-14) "Maurice" served in office longer than any other Handsome Dan; he was the only holder of the office to come out of retirement to serve again, due to the death of his successor, "Whizzer".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:1-14)

In December 1988, he was hit by a car near [East Rock Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Rock_Park "East Rock Park") and needed 3 pins in his hip for recovery.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:1-14) He appeared in _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ in 1989.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] At one point, Getman auctioned off the right to walk Maurice at the next Harvard football game for $1,500.

His patience with the tedium of posing for professional [photographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photographer "Photographer") also served him well as he posed for game programs, [brochures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brochure "Brochure"), and the 1991 Yale [Christmas card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_card "Christmas card"), wearing a [wreath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreath "Wreath") and [Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") hat.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:1-14) He also appeared at swim meets, wearing a bathing suit.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:1-14) Maurice would sing along with the Yale [fight song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_song "Fight song") (at least the "bow wow wow" part); he would "play dead" when asked whether he would rather die or join Harvard; and he lost his normally docile nature around mascots of opposing teams, launching assaults on the Princeton tiger mascot and the [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University") bear mascot.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He died in 1997, just before turning 14.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Handsome Dan XIV

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XIV")]

Active 1995–1996 (died of heart attack).  
 "Whizzer" _aka_ "Hetherbull", also owned by Chris Getman, was donated by Yale alumnus and bulldog breeder [Bob Hetherington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hetherington "Bob Hetherington") and was a descendant of 52-time [best-in-show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformation_show "Conformation show") winner [Hetherbull Arrogant Frigott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hetherbull_Arrogant_Frigott?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hetherbull Arrogant Frigott (page does not exist)"). He possessed a [temperament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperament "Temperament") so [hyperexcitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperexcitable?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hyperexcitable (page does not exist)") that he died in office from a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction "Myocardial infarction"), and was succeeded by his predecessor and housemate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Handsome Dan XV

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XV")]

Active 1996–2005 (unknown death).  
 "Louis", also donated by Bob Hetherington and owned by Chris Getman, was named after three people named Louis, including football coach [Carm Louis Cozza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carm_Cozza "Carm Cozza"). He died in office in January 2005 of a possible heart attack.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)

## Handsome Dan XVI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XVI")]

Active 2005–2006 (retired).  
 Handsome Dan XVI was chosen on 26 April 2005. Magnificent Mugsy Rangoon, a Bulldog from [Hamden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamden,_Connecticut "Hamden, Connecticut"), was picked by a five-person panel for his gregarious personality, large size (69 pounds),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2) good health, and his ability to deal with the raucous [Yale Precision Marching Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Precision_Marching_Band "Yale Precision Marching Band"). At the auditions, Mugsy gained great favor by focusing on a crimson blanket (representing Harvard) versus the stuffed-toy tiger (representing [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University")).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2) "We beat Princeton three of four years," said Jeff Mroz, Yale's quarterback. "We want to beat Harvard."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)

Mugsy is owned by Bob Sansone, a [North Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Haven,_Connecticut "North Haven, Connecticut") middle school teacher.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-15)

At his first [Harvard-Yale Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard-Yale_football_games_(The_Game) "Harvard-Yale football games (The Game)") in 2005, Handsome Dan XVI was briefly stolen by a pair of Harvard undergraduates, in response to a Yale student stealing the Harvard flag and running across the field back to the Yale side with it. The two lured him into the Harvard [student section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_section "Student section") of the [Yale Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Bowl "Yale Bowl") as he chewed a toy depicting a Harvard football player. Yale University Police recovered him, unharmed but without his Yale sweater, a few minutes later.

Handsome Dans traditionally reign for a lifetime, but Mugsy retired and lived with his owner Bob Sansone in Hamden.

## Handsome Dan XVII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XVII")]

Active 2006–2016 (died of heart attack).

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Inflatable_Handsome_Dan.jpg/250px-Inflatable_Handsome_Dan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inflatable_Handsome_Dan.jpg)

An inflatable Handsome Dan bulldog, on display during the 2007 Harvard-Yale game

A new bulldog named Sherman quietly assumed the mascot position as Handsome Dan XVII in late winter 2006.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:0-16)

Bred by Diane Judy of Johnson City, Tenn., Handsome Dan XVII, a 50-pound bulldog, was the half brother of Rambo, owned by former Yale football captain Rory Hennessey.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-:0-16) His home name was "Sherman", after the [tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_Sherman "M4 Sherman") and Connecticut icon [Roger Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Sherman "Roger Sherman"). He took over as Handsome Dan XVII with great enthusiasm. He was photographed with former president [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") and Sir [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney"). He was very athletic, retrieved with vigor and raised thousands of dollars for charity.

He died on August 11, 2016.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-17)

## Handsome Dan XVIII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XVIII")]

Active 2016–2021 (retired).  
 Handsome Dan XVIII was announced as mascot on November 17, 2016. He was born September 23, 2016, to breeders Jessica and Pete Seiders of Wicked Good Bulldogges in Maine. After generations of English Bulldog mascots, the university chose a healthier breed and closer replication of the original Handsome Dan. Handsome Dan XVIII was an Olde English Bulldogge, also known as a Victorian Bulldog, a recreation of the Victorian Era Bulldog bred for health and temperament. Handsome Dan XVIII's football record was 3–1 against Harvard and 24–7 overall through the 2019 season. The new keeper of the mascot, called Walter at home, was Kevin Discepolo (Yale ’09), a former lacrosse player turned Yale’s assistant athletic director of facilities, operations, and events.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-19)

On 5 November 2020, it was announced that Handsome Dan XVIII would retire in early spring 2021 following the October departure of Discepolo, though it was not known whether there was a causal link.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-20)

## Handsome Dan XIX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XIX")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Handsome_Dan_Kingman.jpg/250px-Handsome_Dan_Kingman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Handsome_Dan_Kingman.jpg)

Handsome Dan XIX (Kingman) (March 2022)

Active 2021–present. Handsome Dan XIX was announced as mascot on March 18, 2021. He was born January 2, 2021, and is a nephew of his predecessor Handsome Dan XVIII. Like his predecessor he is an Olde English Bulldogge aka Victorian Bulldog produced by Jessica and Pete Seiders of Wicked Good Bulldogges from Maine.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-XIXannouncement-21) In addition to being known as Handsome Dan, he was named "Kingman" by his handler, Kassandra “Kassie” Haro, after [the late Yale president of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingman_Brewster_Jr. "Kingman Brewster Jr.").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-23)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

The [Shake Shack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_Shack "Shake Shack") location in New Haven, Connecticut, features a menu item named after Handsome Dan, called the Handsome Dog.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-24) The Handsome Dog, which features beer-marinated deep-fried onions and two kinds of cheese, debuted at the New Haven location but can now be found at all other Shake Shack locations, albeit as the Dapper Dog.

The TV series _[Gilmore Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilmore\_Girls "Gilmore Girls")_, which is set in Connecticut, makes several references to the Handsome Dan Statue.

In the TV series _[Gossip Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gossip\_Girl "Gossip Girl")_, Blair Waldorf is given a pet bulldog by her father in season 2, episode 16. The bulldog is named Handsome Dan in honor of Blair's aspirations to attend Yale following high school. Blair shortens his name to "Handsome". Blair's scheming results in her losing her acceptance to Yale, and she gives the bulldog away to a homeless man. However, she later orders him back. When her father returns to France, he forces his daughter to let him take “Handsome” back with him, as he is disappointed with her.

In the movie _[Wayne's World 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne's\_World\_2 "Wayne's World 2")_, Handsome Dan is a radio personality for WPIG. Despite his name, he isn't classically handsome. Harry Shearer played the role.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Mascot of Yale University's sports teams

**Handsome Dan** is a [bulldog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulldog "Bulldog") that serves as the [mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot "Mascot") of [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")'s sports teams. In addition to a person wearing a [costume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume "Costume"), the position is filled by an actual bulldog, the honor and title being transferred to a successor upon death or retirement.

## Handsome Dan I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Handsome Dan I")]

Active 1889–1897 (retired to England).

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale%27s_mascot.jpg/250px-Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale%27s_mascot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Original_Handsome_Dan_Yale's_mascot.jpg)

The original Handsome Dan, bought by [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") tackle Andrew Graves in 1889

Handsome Dan was selected based on his ability to tolerate bands and children, negative reaction to the color [crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimson "Crimson") and to [tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigers "Tigers") (the symbols of rival schools [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard "Harvard") and [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") respectively), bought by Yale student Andrew Barbey Graves,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) who cleaned up the dog and named him “Handsome Dan.” Soon, Dan followed Graves everywhere around campus, including sporting events.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The students quickly adopted Dan as the Yale mascot. After Graves graduated and returned to England, Dan stayed on campus with his master's brother, William Leon Graves.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) Before football and baseball games would begin, Handsome Dan founded a tradition and a dynasty by being led across the field. One newspaper reported: "He was a big white bulldog, with one of the greatest faces a dog of that breed (English) ever carried". This was not an exaggeration, as Handsome Dan was one of the finest specimens of his breed in America, and went on to win first prize at the [Westminster Dog Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Dog_Show "Westminster Dog Show") and at least thirty other first prize ribbons in the United States and Canada.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tim_Cohane_pp._72-73-4) According to the [Hartford Courant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford_Courant "Hartford Courant"), "In personal appearance, he seemed like a cross between an alligator and a horned frog, and he was called handsome by the metaphysicians under the law of compensation. The title came to him, he never sought it. He was always taken to games on a leash, and the Harvard football team for years owed its continued existence to the fact that the rope held."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The Philadelphia Press reported that "a favorite trick was to tell him to 'Speak to Harvard.' He would bark ferociously and work himself into physical contortions of rage never before dreamed of by a dog. Dan was peculiar to himself in one thing – he would never associate with anyone but students. Dan implanted himself more firmly in the hearts of Yale students than any mascot had ever done before."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) Handsome Dan crossed the Atlantic to join his old master in 1897 and died in 1898. Graves had Dan [taxidermied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxidermy "Taxidermy") and returned him to be displayed at Yale in the old gymnasium. When it was torn down, Dan I was sent to the [Peabody Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History "Peabody Museum of Natural History") for reconstruction. Handsome Dan I now is in a sealed glass case in one of the trophy rooms of Yale's [Payne Whitney Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payne_Whitney_Gymnasium "Payne Whitney Gymnasium"), where, according to Stanton Ford, "he is the perpetual guardian of the treasures which attest to generations of Yale athletic glory." Andrew Graves died of [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") on February 18, 1948, in Westbury, Long Island.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-5)

## Handsome Dan II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Handsome Dan II")]

Active 1933–1937 (died of a broken leg).  
 After a 35-year interval, Handsome Dan II was purchased with pennies donated by the freshman class, and given to [coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(sport) "Coach (sport)")[Ducky Pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ducky_Pond "Ducky Pond").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) Handsome Dan II was [dognapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dognapping "Dognapping") by Harvard students the day before the 1934 [Harvard-Yale football game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard-Yale_football_games_(The_Game) "Harvard-Yale football games (The Game)"), and Yale students were alarmed at photographs of him happily seated at the foot of the statue of [John Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvard_(clergyman) "John Harvard (clergyman)") in [Harvard Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard "Harvard Yard"), having a snack.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) He died of a leg fracture received from a jump. Handsome Dan II is now located at the Yale Peabody Museum.

## Handsome Dan III

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Handsome Dan III")]

Active 1937–1938 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Handsome Dan III was a huge white dog who exhibited morbid [fear of crowds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoraphobia "Agoraphobia") and had to be retired.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIII-7)

## Handsome Dan IV

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Handsome Dan IV")]

Active 1938–1940 (retired due to injury).  
 Handsome Dan IV had his spine fractured by a car early in his term of office, leaving his hind legs paralyzed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8) Until he eventually died in 1940, a bulldog named Bull served in his place, becoming Handsome Dan V.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8)

## Handsome Dan V

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Handsome Dan V")]

Active 1940–1947 (died of old age).  
 "Bull", brought in his youth to watch football practices by his owner, high school student Bob Day, who lived near the [Yale Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Bowl "Yale Bowl"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanV-9) ascended to office when Handsome Dan IV died.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIV-8) A great success, he loved public appearances and the adulation of crowds, was a familiar figure around the [locker rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locker_room "Locker room"), and joined the team on a trip to [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanV-9)

## Handsome Dan VI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VI")]

Active 1947–1949 (died at age two).  
 Handsome Dan VI was eight weeks old when he took the role, but died at age two.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVI-10) It was reported that he died from fear of [fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks") at the Yale-Harvard game, or of shame from seeing the Yale team lose to both Princeton and Harvard in the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVI-10)

## Handsome Dan VII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VII")]

Active 1949–1952 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Handsome Dan VII was donated to football coach [Herman Hickman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Hickman "Herman Hickman") at age 3 but he proved to have a bad temper, which suited him better in his next position as a watchdog on a [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") estate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVII-11)

## Handsome Dan VIII

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Handsome Dan VIII")]

Active 1952 (retired due to emotional instability).  
 Up to this point, Handsome Dans had lived at the Yale Boathouse and were cared for in a somewhat haphazard fashion. Handsome Dan VIII, however, was owned by assistant football manager Tom Shutt,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVIII-12) ushering in a new era of family membership for the office-holder. Nevertheless, he had to retire after only two games due to intense discomfort with public appearances.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanVIII-12)

## Handsome Dan IX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Handsome Dan IX")]

Active 1953–1959 (died of acute [kidney disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_disease "Kidney disease")).  
 Notable for falling off the dock at the Yale Boathouse and nearly drowning[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) (confirming the hypothesis that bulldogs cannot swim, due to the peculiarities of their physiques); some contemporary news reports say that he had to be [resuscitated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resuscitate "Resuscitate") after having had his head embedded in the mud.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) He also appeared on the cover of _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ magazine in November, 1956. "Danny" was born September 11, 1953, and owned by John E. Sanders, Assistant Professor of Geology, after an earlier custody by physical education instructor Alfred E. Scholz and Varsity Crew Coach Jim Rothschmidt.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13) He made his mascot debut at the age of six weeks and an [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") at his death revealed that he succumbed to acute [nephrotic syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nephrotic_syndrome "Nephrotic syndrome").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIX-13)

## Handsome Dan X

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Handsome Dan X")]

Active 1959–1969 (retired due to old age).  
 "Woodie" _aka_ "Boodnick", also owned by John E. Sanders, marked a return to the high standards seen in Handsome Dan V. An impressive 74 pounds, a beloved family pet as well as winner of the best bulldog title at the [Cape Cod Kennel Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Kennel_Club?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cape Cod Kennel Club (page does not exist)")[conformation dog show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformation_dog_show "Conformation dog show"), he was instrumental in leading Yale's football team to its 9 and 0 season in 1960. He spent several years commuting to New Haven, CT, from Dobbs Ferry, NY, prior to his retirement. His registered AKC kennel name was "Bayside Woodnought." He was sired by Ch. Bonny Boy of Fearnought out of Woodside's Christie Lou, and was a grandson of the famed Kippax Fearnought, the celebrated English import, who went Best in Show in 1955 at Westminster. He died in 1971 of natural causes.

## Handsome Dan XI

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Handsome_Dan&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Handsome Dan XI")]

Active 1969–1974 (retired due to [arthritis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthritis "Arthritis")).  
 "Oliver", owned by Yale's Pierson College master [John Hersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hersey "John Hersey"), loved football but had a tendency to doze in the sun during games. He was frequently sighted on [Martha's Vineyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha's_Vineyard "Martha's Vineyard") during the tourist season.

## Handsome Dan XII

Active 1975–1984.  
 "Bingo", owned by history professor [Rollin G. Osterweis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rollin_G._Osterweis "Rollin G. Osterweis"), was described by her owner as "pugnacious and stubborn, but lovable."[_[quote needs citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Inline\_citation#When\_you\_must\_use\_inline\_citations "Wikipedia:Inline citation")_] Bingo also had the distinction of being the only female Handsome Dan. Bingo was stolen by four Princeton undergrads posing as Yale cheerleaders. They took Bingo to a friend's apartment in New York City on the run from authorities.
