## Personal names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_biblical_names&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal names")]

Personal names play a variety of roles in the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible"). They sometimes relate to the nominee's role in a [biblical narrative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_of_the_Bible "Books of the Bible"), as in the case of [Nabal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabal "Nabal"), a foolish man whose name means "fool".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Biblical_names#cite_note-1) Names in the Bible can represent human hopes, [divine revelations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_revelation "Divine revelation"), or are used to illustrate [prophecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophecies "Prophecies").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Biblical_names#cite_note-2)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

The titles given to characters, locations, and entities in the Bible can differ across various English translations. In a study conducted by the BibleAsk team in 2024, a comprehensive catalog of names found in the King James Version was compiled and organized into categories such as individuals, geographical locations, national groups, and miscellaneous designations. The team discovered that within the King James Version Bible, a total of 3,418 distinct names were identified. Among these, 1,940 names pertain to individuals, 1,072 names refer to places, 317 names denote collective entities or nations, and 66 names are allocated to miscellaneous items such as months, rivers, or pagan deities. There are instances of overlap, where the same name may be used across multiple categories (e.g., as both a personal name and a geographical location).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Biblical_names#cite_note-3)

### Most popular names in ancient Judaea

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_biblical_names&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Most popular names in ancient Judaea")]

Based on a database of 3000 names documented from written sources dating from 330 BC – AD 200 (from [Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great")'s [conquest through the Hasmonean kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Palestine_region#Hellenistic_period_and_the_Kingdom_of_Hasmonean_Judea "Timeline of the Palestine region") and most of the [Roman period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Palestine_region#Roman_period "Timeline of the Palestine region")), the most common twelve male names among [Palestinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_(region) "Palestine (region)") Jews were:[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Biblical_names#cite_note-Bauckham2017-4)

*   1. Simon/Simeon (243)
*   2. Joseph/Joses (218)
*   3. Lazarus/Eleazar (166)
*   4. Judas/Judah (164)
*   5. John/Yohanan (122)
*   6. Jesus/Joshua (99)
*   7. Ananias/Hananiah (82)
*   8. Jonathan (71)
*   9. Matthew/Matthias/Mattathias (62)
*   10. Manaen/Menahem (42)
*   11. James/Jacob (40)
*   12. Annas/Hanan (35)

During this period, the most common twelve female names were:[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Biblical_names#cite_note-Bauckham2017-4)

*   1. Mary/Mariam (70)
*   2. Salome (58)
*   3. Shelamzion (24)
*   4. Martha (20)
*   5. Joanna (12)
*   5. Sapphira/Shiphra (12)
*   7. Berenice (8)
*   8. Imma (7)
*   8. Mara (7)
*   10. Cyprus (6)
*   10. Sarah (6)
*   10. Alexandra (6)

Protagonist of the Book of Ruth in the Hebrew Bible

**Ruth** ([/r uː θ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): רוּת, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Hebrew "Romanization of Hebrew"):_rûṯ_) is the person after whom the [Book of Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Ruth "Book of Ruth") is named. She was a [Moabite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moab "Moab") woman who married an Israelite, [Mahlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_and_Chilion "Mahlon and Chilion"). After the death of all the male members of her family (her husband, her father-in-law, and her brother-in-law), she stayed with her mother-in-law, [Naomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_(biblical_figure) "Naomi (biblical figure)"), and moved to Judah with her, where Ruth won the love and protection of a wealthy relative, [Boaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boaz "Boaz"), through her kindness.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-ppp-1) She is the great-grandmother of [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David "David").

The story of Ruth as told in the Book of Ruth was likely written in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Hebrew "Biblical Hebrew") during the [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Empire "Persian Empire") period (550–330 BCE).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-3) Some scholars generally consider the book to be a work of [historical fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_fiction "Historical fiction"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-5) while other scholars, including [evangelical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical "Evangelical") scholars, hold that it is a [historical narrative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_narrative "Historical narrative") written in the form of a short story.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-6)

## Book of Ruth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Book of Ruth")]

In the days when the [judges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_judges "Biblical judges") were leading the [tribes of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_of_Israel "Tribes of Israel"), there was a famine. Because of this crisis, [Elimelech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elimelech "Elimelech"), a man from [Bethlehem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem "Bethlehem") in Judah, moved to [Moab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moab "Moab") with his wife, [Naomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_(biblical_figure) "Naomi (biblical figure)"), and his two sons, [Mahlon and Chilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_and_Chilion "Mahlon and Chilion"). There Elimelech died, and the two sons married Moabite women, Ruth and [Orpah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpah "Orpah"). They lived for about ten years in Moab, before Mahlon and Chilion also died.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg/250px-Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg)

Detail of a stained-glass window by [Henry Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Holiday "Henry Holiday") in [Salisbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Cathedral "Salisbury Cathedral") (1880)

Naomi heard that the famine in Judah had passed and decided to return home. She told her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' houses and marry again. At first, both Orpah and Ruth refused to leave her, but Naomi told them that she was unlikely to have more sons that Orpah and Ruth could [marry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yibbum "Yibbum"). They all wept, and Orpah decided to leave Naomi and return to her people. Naomi tried again to send Ruth back, too, but she told her that "(...) where you go I will go, and where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried." ([ESV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Standard_Version "English Standard Version")) In the [Targum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targum "Targum"), each of Ruth's lines is preceded by Naomi, who defines what it is to be Jewish.

Eventually, Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") harvest. Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, lived nearby, and Ruth decided to go to his field and [glean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleaning "Gleaning") after his [reapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaping "Reaping"). When Boaz arrived at the field, he asked who the young woman was, and then told Ruth not to go to anyone else's field, but keep gleaning there. He told her that if she was thirsty, she could drink from the vessels of the female reapers, but to avoid the men. When Ruth asked him why he was so good to a foreigner, Boaz told her that he had heard how loyal she was to Naomi. At mealtime, Boaz invited Ruth to eat with him, and then instructed his male reapers to not reproach or rebuke her, and even to pull out some barley from their bundles and leave it for her to glean. Ruth gleaned at the fields of Boaz throughout the barley and wheat harvests.

When the harvest ended, and Boaz was [winnowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnowing "Winnowing") barley at night at the [threshing floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threshing_floor "Threshing floor"), Naomi advised Ruth to wash and anoint herself, go to the threshing floor, and when Boaz had lain down to sleep, uncover his feet and lie down there. Ruth did as she said. At midnight, Boaz woke up, and Ruth asked him to protect her, as he was her husband's [goel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goel_(Judaism) "Goel (Judaism)"), closest relative tasked with protecting his rights. Boaz said that he would like to do so, but Ruth had an even closer relative than him.

In the morning, Boaz went and sat down by the gates of the town, then talked to the relative when he arrived. He told him that Naomi was selling Elimelech's land. The man said that he would redeem it. Boaz then says that one of them will acquire Ruth, although the text is unclear due to a [Qere and Ketiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qere_and_Ketiv "Qere and Ketiv") disagreement. In the Qere, spoken form, the relative would acquire Ruth. In the Ketiv, written form, Boaz would acquire Ruth. In both cases, it would be to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance in a [levirate marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levirate_marriage "Levirate marriage"). The man refused to redeem the land, fearing that it would impair his own inheritance. Boaz then redeemed the land and acquired Ruth. Ruth became Boaz's wife, and bore him a son. After Ruth had given birth, Naomi took the child to her breast. The women of Bethlehem named him [Obed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obed_(biblical_figure) "Obed (biblical figure)") and said that Naomi had borne a son. Obed became the father of [Jesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_(biblical_figure) "Jesse (biblical figure)"), the father of [King David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_David "King David").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-ppp-1)

## Religious interpretations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Religious interpretations")]

### Jewish perspectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Jewish perspectives")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg/250px-RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg)

Boaz and Ruth by [Rembrandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rembrandt "Rembrandt")

Boaz of Judah blessed Ruth for her extraordinary kindness both to Naomi of Judah and to the Judean People (Ruth 3:10). "And he [Boaz] said, 'May you be blessed of the Lord, my daughter; your latest act of kindness is greater than the first, not to follow the young men, whether poor or rich.'" Commentary of Rashi (c.1040–1105) regarding the first act of kindness: "that you did with your mother-in-law".

Ruth's kindness as noted in the Book of Ruth by Boaz is seen in the Jewish Tradition as in rare contradistinction to the peoples of Moab (where Ruth comes from) and Amon in general, who were noted by the Torah for their distinct _lack_ of kindness. Deut. 23:5: "Because they [the peoples of Amon and Moab] did not greet you with bread and water on the way when you left Egypt, and because he [the people of Moab] hired Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor in Aram Naharaim against you, to curse you." Rashi notes regarding Israel's travels on the way: "when you were in [a state of] extreme exhaustion."

According to the [Ruth Rabbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Rabbah "Ruth Rabbah"), Ruth was Orpah's sister and the two were daughters of [Eglon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eglon_(king) "Eglon (king)"), the king of Moab; according to the same text, Eglon was the son of [Balak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balak "Balak").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) Tamar Meir of the [Jewish Women's Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Women's_Archive "Jewish Women's Archive") writes that Ruth and David being descended from these two men is seen as a "reward" for them.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) For Balak, it is his reward for building altars and for Eglon, it is his reward for "arising upon hearing the name of God from Ehud son of Gera".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) The same text says Ruth did not convert during her marriage to Mahlon, contradicting other rabbinic literature, which says Ruth formally converted to Judaism for the sake of marrying Mahlon but did not fully accept the faith until later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7)

[Josephus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josephus "Josephus") viewed the Book of Ruth as historical and referenced it in his _[Antiquities of the Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities\_of\_the\_Jews "Antiquities of the Jews")_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-8) Yitzhak Berger suggests Naomi's plan was that Ruth [seduce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seduction "Seduction") Boaz, just as [Tamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_(Genesis) "Tamar (Genesis)") and [Lot's daughters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lot's_daughters "Lot's daughters") all seduced "an older family member in order to become the mother of his offspring". At the crucial moment, however, "Ruth abandons the attempt at seduction and instead requests a permanent, _legal_ union with Boaz."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-9)

### Christian perspectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christian perspectives")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg/250px-1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg)

Ruth and Naomi by [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake")

Ruth is one of five women mentioned in the [genealogy of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genealogy_of_Jesus "Genealogy of Jesus") found in the [Gospel of Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew "Gospel of Matthew"), alongside [Tamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_(Genesis) "Tamar (Genesis)"), [Rahab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahab "Rahab"), the "wife of [Uriah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uriah_the_Hittite "Uriah the Hittite")" ([Bathsheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathsheba "Bathsheba")), and [Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus "Mary, mother of Jesus").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-CBQ-10)[Katharine Doob Sakenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharine_Doob_Sakenfeld "Katharine Doob Sakenfeld") argues that Ruth is a model of loving-kindness (_[hesed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesed "Hesed")_): she acts in ways that promote the well-being of others.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11) In [Ruth 1:8–18](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%201:8%E2%80%9318&version=nrsv), she demonstrated _hesed_ by not going back to Moab but accompanying her mother-in-law to a foreign land.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11) She chose to glean, despite the danger she faced in the field ([Ruth 2:15](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%202:15&version=nrsv)) and the lower social status of the job. Finally, Ruth agrees with Naomi's plan to marry Boaz, even though she was free of family obligations, once again demonstrating her loyalty and obedience ([Ruth 3:10](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%203:10&version=nrsv)).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11)

[Barry Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_G._Webb "Barry G. Webb") argues that in the book, Ruth plays a key role in Naomi's rehabilitation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-12)

Ruth is commemorated as a matriarch in the [Calendar of Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_Saints_(Lutheran) "Calendar of Saints (Lutheran)") of the [Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran_Church%E2%80%93Missouri_Synod "Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod") on 16 July.

She can also be seen as a prototype of a convert to Judaism.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-13)

## Tomb of Ruth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of Ruth")]

Main article: [Tomb of Jesse and Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth "Tomb of Jesse and Ruth")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg/330px-Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg)

Tomb of Jesse and Ruth in Hebron

The traditional burial place of Ruth is a building located in [Hebron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron "Hebron"). [Francesco Quaresmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscus_Quaresmius "Franciscus Quaresmius") in the early 17th century reported that Turks and Orientals generally believed the structure contained the tombs of Jesse and Ruth.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-FQ-15) According to [Moshe Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshe_Sharon "Moshe Sharon"), the association of the site with Ruth is very late, starting in the 19th century.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-MSharon-16) It receives numerous visitors every year, especially on the Jewish holiday of [Shavuot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shavuot "Shavuot"), when the Book of Ruth is read.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-17) Haim Horwitz in his 1835 book on Israeli holy sites _Love of Jerusalem_[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-18) discusses the oral tradition that the tomb houses Ruth's grave as well as Jesse's, who is mentioned in earlier writings. Menachem Mendel of Kamenitz[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-19) wrote in 1839, "Also in the vineyard was a shelter with two graves: one of Jesse, father of David, and one of Ruth, the Moabite."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-20)

## Cultural influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Cultural influence")]

Ruth is one of the Five Heroines of the [Order of the Eastern Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Eastern_Star "Order of the Eastern Star").

Ruth was played by [Elana Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Eden "Elana Eden") in [Henry Koster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Koster "Henry Koster")'s _[The Story of Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_of\_Ruth "The Story of Ruth")_ (1960); the film depicts Ruth as a pagan priestess prior to her religious conversion.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-nyt-21) Sherry Morris portrayed her in _[The Book of Ruth: Journey of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Book\_of\_Ruth:\_Journey\_of\_Faith "The Book of Ruth: Journey of Faith")_ (2009).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-22)

In English literature, [John Keats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats "John Keats") in "[Ode to a Nightingale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode_to_a_Nightingale "Ode to a Nightingale")" references Ruth as isolated and grief-stricken when laboring in exile: "Perhaps the self-same song that found a path/Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,/She stood in tears amid the alien corn;"[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-23)

Protagonist of the Book of Ruth in the Hebrew Bible

| Ruth 𐤓𐤅𐤕 רוּת |

| [![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Hayez_A_woman_as_Ruth.jpg/250px-Hayez_A_woman_as_Ruth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hayez_A_woman_as_Ruth.jpg) _Ruth_ by [Francesco Hayez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Hayez "Francesco Hayez"), 1835 |

**Ruth** ([/r uː θ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): רוּת, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Hebrew "Romanization of Hebrew"):_rûṯ_) is the person after whom the [Book of Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Ruth "Book of Ruth") is named. She was a [Moabite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moab "Moab") woman who married an Israelite, [Mahlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_and_Chilion "Mahlon and Chilion"). After the death of all the male members of her family (her husband, her father-in-law, and her brother-in-law), she stayed with her mother-in-law, [Naomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_(biblical_figure) "Naomi (biblical figure)"), and moved to Judah with her, where Ruth won the love and protection of a wealthy relative, [Boaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boaz "Boaz"), through her kindness.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-ppp-1) She is the great-grandmother of [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David "David").

The story of Ruth as told in the Book of Ruth was likely written in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Hebrew "Biblical Hebrew") during the [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Empire "Persian Empire") period (550–330 BCE).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-3) Some scholars generally consider the book to be a work of [historical fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_fiction "Historical fiction"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-5) while other scholars, including [evangelical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical "Evangelical") scholars, hold that it is a [historical narrative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_narrative "Historical narrative") written in the form of a short story.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-6)

## Book of Ruth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Book of Ruth")]

In the days when the [judges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_judges "Biblical judges") were leading the [tribes of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_of_Israel "Tribes of Israel"), there was a famine. Because of this crisis, [Elimelech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elimelech "Elimelech"), a man from [Bethlehem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem "Bethlehem") in Judah, moved to [Moab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moab "Moab") with his wife, [Naomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_(biblical_figure) "Naomi (biblical figure)"), and his two sons, [Mahlon and Chilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_and_Chilion "Mahlon and Chilion"). There Elimelech died, and the two sons married Moabite women, Ruth and [Orpah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpah "Orpah"). They lived for about ten years in Moab, before Mahlon and Chilion also died.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg/250px-Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salisbury_Cathedral_glass_8.jpg)

Detail of a stained-glass window by [Henry Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Holiday "Henry Holiday") in [Salisbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Cathedral "Salisbury Cathedral") (1880)

Naomi heard that the famine in Judah had passed and decided to return home. She told her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' houses and marry again. At first, both Orpah and Ruth refused to leave her, but Naomi told them that she was unlikely to have more sons that Orpah and Ruth could [marry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yibbum "Yibbum"). They all wept, and Orpah decided to leave Naomi and return to her people. Naomi tried again to send Ruth back, too, but she told her that "(...) where you go I will go, and where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried." ([ESV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Standard_Version "English Standard Version")) In the [Targum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targum "Targum"), each of Ruth's lines is preceded by Naomi, who defines what it is to be Jewish.

Eventually, Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") harvest. Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, lived nearby, and Ruth decided to go to his field and [glean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleaning "Gleaning") after his [reapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaping "Reaping"). When Boaz arrived at the field, he asked who the young woman was, and then told Ruth not to go to anyone else's field, but keep gleaning there. He told her that if she was thirsty, she could drink from the vessels of the female reapers, but to avoid the men. When Ruth asked him why he was so good to a foreigner, Boaz told her that he had heard how loyal she was to Naomi. At mealtime, Boaz invited Ruth to eat with him, and then instructed his male reapers to not reproach or rebuke her, and even to pull out some barley from their bundles and leave it for her to glean. Ruth gleaned at the fields of Boaz throughout the barley and wheat harvests.

When the harvest ended, and Boaz was [winnowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnowing "Winnowing") barley at night at the [threshing floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threshing_floor "Threshing floor"), Naomi advised Ruth to wash and anoint herself, go to the threshing floor, and when Boaz had lain down to sleep, uncover his feet and lie down there. Ruth did as she said. At midnight, Boaz woke up, and Ruth asked him to protect her, as he was her husband's [goel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goel_(Judaism) "Goel (Judaism)"), closest relative tasked with protecting his rights. Boaz said that he would like to do so, but Ruth had an even closer relative than him.

In the morning, Boaz went and sat down by the gates of the town, then talked to the relative when he arrived. He told him that Naomi was selling Elimelech's land. The man said that he would redeem it. Boaz then says that one of them will acquire Ruth, although the text is unclear due to a [Qere and Ketiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qere_and_Ketiv "Qere and Ketiv") disagreement. In the Qere, spoken form, the relative would acquire Ruth. In the Ketiv, written form, Boaz would acquire Ruth. In both cases, it would be to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance in a [levirate marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levirate_marriage "Levirate marriage"). The man refused to redeem the land, fearing that it would impair his own inheritance. Boaz then redeemed the land and acquired Ruth. Ruth became Boaz's wife, and bore him a son. After Ruth had given birth, Naomi took the child to her breast. The women of Bethlehem named him [Obed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obed_(biblical_figure) "Obed (biblical figure)") and said that Naomi had borne a son. Obed became the father of [Jesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_(biblical_figure) "Jesse (biblical figure)"), the father of [King David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_David "King David").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-ppp-1)

## Religious interpretations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Religious interpretations")]

### Jewish perspectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Jewish perspectives")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg/250px-RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RembrandtBoasRuth.jpg)

Boaz and Ruth by [Rembrandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rembrandt "Rembrandt")

Boaz of Judah blessed Ruth for her extraordinary kindness both to Naomi of Judah and to the Judean People (Ruth 3:10). "And he [Boaz] said, 'May you be blessed of the Lord, my daughter; your latest act of kindness is greater than the first, not to follow the young men, whether poor or rich.'" Commentary of Rashi (c.1040–1105) regarding the first act of kindness: "that you did with your mother-in-law".

Ruth's kindness as noted in the Book of Ruth by Boaz is seen in the Jewish Tradition as in rare contradistinction to the peoples of Moab (where Ruth comes from) and Amon in general, who were noted by the Torah for their distinct _lack_ of kindness. Deut. 23:5: "Because they [the peoples of Amon and Moab] did not greet you with bread and water on the way when you left Egypt, and because he [the people of Moab] hired Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor in Aram Naharaim against you, to curse you." Rashi notes regarding Israel's travels on the way: "when you were in [a state of] extreme exhaustion."

According to the [Ruth Rabbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Rabbah "Ruth Rabbah"), Ruth was Orpah's sister and the two were daughters of [Eglon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eglon_(king) "Eglon (king)"), the king of Moab; according to the same text, Eglon was the son of [Balak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balak "Balak").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) Tamar Meir of the [Jewish Women's Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Women's_Archive "Jewish Women's Archive") writes that Ruth and David being descended from these two men is seen as a "reward" for them.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) For Balak, it is his reward for building altars and for Eglon, it is his reward for "arising upon hearing the name of God from Ehud son of Gera".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7) The same text says Ruth did not convert during her marriage to Mahlon, contradicting other rabbinic literature, which says Ruth formally converted to Judaism for the sake of marrying Mahlon but did not fully accept the faith until later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-jw-7)

[Josephus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josephus "Josephus") viewed the Book of Ruth as historical and referenced it in his _[Antiquities of the Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities\_of\_the\_Jews "Antiquities of the Jews")_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-8) Yitzhak Berger suggests Naomi's plan was that Ruth [seduce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seduction "Seduction") Boaz, just as [Tamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_(Genesis) "Tamar (Genesis)") and [Lot's daughters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lot's_daughters "Lot's daughters") all seduced "an older family member in order to become the mother of his offspring". At the crucial moment, however, "Ruth abandons the attempt at seduction and instead requests a permanent, _legal_ union with Boaz."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-9)

### Christian perspectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christian perspectives")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg/250px-1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1795-William-Blake-Naomi-entreating-Ruth-Orpah.jpg)

Ruth and Naomi by [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake")

Ruth is one of five women mentioned in the [genealogy of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genealogy_of_Jesus "Genealogy of Jesus") found in the [Gospel of Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew "Gospel of Matthew"), alongside [Tamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_(Genesis) "Tamar (Genesis)"), [Rahab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahab "Rahab"), the "wife of [Uriah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uriah_the_Hittite "Uriah the Hittite")" ([Bathsheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathsheba "Bathsheba")), and [Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus "Mary, mother of Jesus").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-CBQ-10)[Katharine Doob Sakenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharine_Doob_Sakenfeld "Katharine Doob Sakenfeld") argues that Ruth is a model of loving-kindness (_[hesed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesed "Hesed")_): she acts in ways that promote the well-being of others.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11) In [Ruth 1:8–18](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%201:8%E2%80%9318&version=nrsv), she demonstrated _hesed_ by not going back to Moab but accompanying her mother-in-law to a foreign land.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11) She chose to glean, despite the danger she faced in the field ([Ruth 2:15](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%202:15&version=nrsv)) and the lower social status of the job. Finally, Ruth agrees with Naomi's plan to marry Boaz, even though she was free of family obligations, once again demonstrating her loyalty and obedience ([Ruth 3:10](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Ruth%203:10&version=nrsv)).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-saken-11)

[Barry Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_G._Webb "Barry G. Webb") argues that in the book, Ruth plays a key role in Naomi's rehabilitation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-12)

Ruth is commemorated as a matriarch in the [Calendar of Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_Saints_(Lutheran) "Calendar of Saints (Lutheran)") of the [Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran_Church%E2%80%93Missouri_Synod "Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod") on 16 July.

She can also be seen as a prototype of a convert to Judaism.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-13)

## Tomb of Ruth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of Ruth")]

Main article: [Tomb of Jesse and Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth "Tomb of Jesse and Ruth")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg/330px-Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomb_of_Jesse_and_Ruth_in_Hebron.jpg)

Tomb of Jesse and Ruth in Hebron

The traditional burial place of Ruth is a building located in [Hebron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron "Hebron"). [Francesco Quaresmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscus_Quaresmius "Franciscus Quaresmius") in the early 17th century reported that Turks and Orientals generally believed the structure contained the tombs of Jesse and Ruth.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-FQ-15) According to [Moshe Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshe_Sharon "Moshe Sharon"), the association of the site with Ruth is very late, starting in the 19th century.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-MSharon-16) It receives numerous visitors every year, especially on the Jewish holiday of [Shavuot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shavuot "Shavuot"), when the Book of Ruth is read.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-17) Haim Horwitz in his 1835 book on Israeli holy sites _Love of Jerusalem_[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-18) discusses the oral tradition that the tomb houses Ruth's grave as well as Jesse's, who is mentioned in earlier writings. Menachem Mendel of Kamenitz[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-19) wrote in 1839, "Also in the vineyard was a shelter with two graves: one of Jesse, father of David, and one of Ruth, the Moabite."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-20)

## Cultural influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ruth_(biblical_figure)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Cultural influence")]

Ruth is one of the Five Heroines of the [Order of the Eastern Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Eastern_Star "Order of the Eastern Star").

Ruth was played by [Elana Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Eden "Elana Eden") in [Henry Koster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Koster "Henry Koster")'s _[The Story of Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_of\_Ruth "The Story of Ruth")_ (1960); the film depicts Ruth as a pagan priestess prior to her religious conversion.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-nyt-21) Sherry Morris portrayed her in _[The Book of Ruth: Journey of Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Book\_of\_Ruth:\_Journey\_of\_Faith "The Book of Ruth: Journey of Faith")_ (2009).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-22)

In English literature, [John Keats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats "John Keats") in "[Ode to a Nightingale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode_to_a_Nightingale "Ode to a Nightingale")" references Ruth as isolated and grief-stricken when laboring in exile: "Perhaps the self-same song that found a path/Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,/She stood in tears amid the alien corn;"[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_(biblical_figure)#cite_note-23)

**Goldy Gopher** is the mascot for the University of Minnesota and the associated sports teams, known as the [Golden Gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers "Minnesota Golden Gophers"), as well as a four-time UCA Mascot National Champion (2011, 2013, 2017, and 2018).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-1) During the year, Goldy makes over 1000 appearances and is at virtually all home games for University teams, usually wearing the appropriate sporting attire. The mascot is based on the [thirteen-lined ground squirrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen-lined_ground_squirrel "Thirteen-lined ground squirrel"), colloquially referred to as a “gopher” in Minnesota.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-2)

## Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Origins")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg/250px-Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg)

The 1857 political cartoon from which Minnesota derived its nickname, "The Gopher State".

[Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") became known as the "Gopher State" in 1857, the result of a political cartoon ridiculing the $5 million Railroad Loan which helped open up the West. The cartoon portrayed shifty railroad barons as [striped gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen-lined_ground_squirrel "Thirteen-lined ground squirrel") pulling a railroad car carrying the Territorial Legislature toward the "Slough of Despond". The first U of M yearbook bearing the name "Gopher Annual" appeared in 1887.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3)

Minnesota's athletic teams became widely known as the "Gophers" by the 1920s, but it was not until 1934 that [Halsey Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halsey_Hall "Halsey Hall"), great Minnesota sportswriter and broadcaster, dubbed [Bernie Bierman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Bierman "Bernie Bierman")'s all-gold uniformed team "The Golden Gophers". Bierman had chosen the gold color because the football blended in with the uniforms.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3)

The embodiment of the Gopher mascot came to life in 1952 when University of Minnesota assistant bandmaster Jerome Glass bought a fuzzy wool gopher suit with a [papier-mâché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papier-m%C3%A2ch%C3%A9 "Papier-mâché") head and asked one of the band members to climb into it.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3) "Goldy" Gopher (the first name seems to have appeared sometime in the 1960s) became a fixture within the [University of Minnesota Marching Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Marching_Band "University of Minnesota Marching Band") and Pep Band, as each year a band member was chosen to don the suit for that season. Wherever these two bands performed, Goldy was there to glad-hand with the crowd, hug the little kids, and torment the cheerleaders.

During the early 1960s, Goldy was written into the football pre-game and halftime shows with a specific place to be. Limited visibility from within the suit made it difficult to see out, and any of the suit's wearers with glasses would fog up while trying to peer out the mouth hole, as the eyeholes were useless. One benefit during the cold games at [Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Stadium_(University_of_Minnesota) "Memorial Stadium (University of Minnesota)") in November was that Goldy Gopher was one of the few fans that stayed warm.

## Attitude and attire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Attitude and attire")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg/250px-Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg)

Goldy Gopher [snowboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowboarding "Snowboarding") down a staircase at a [women's volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers_women's_volleyball "Minnesota Golden Gophers women's volleyball") game

Each band member who was allowed the joy of being the Gopher developed an individual personality, a unique way of relating to the crowd. The mystique of Goldy Gopher became a tradition that absolutely prohibited removal of the head while in public, maintaining an illusion for the younger children that Goldy Gopher was a real live huggable animal.

From 1952 until 1990, the Gopher appearing at U of M sports events was a member of the Marching Band, and a symbiosis developed through the years that on more than one occasion kept Goldy out of trouble. With a propensity for attracting tail-pulling kids, Goldy relied on the band to save the gopher from their clutches. And when the opposing team's cheerleaders or band members managed to “kidnap” the unfortunate rodent (a [Big Ten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference") tradition), band members would come to the rescue.

In the late 1980s the U of M Athletic Department began to make use of Goldy at an ever-increasing number of events, and held University-wide tryouts to secure a number of students who could cover the busy schedule. The Athletic Department's Spirit Squad officially took charge of Goldy in 1992.

A signature move of Goldy's is head spinning, usually brought on by crowd chants of "Spin your head!", a tradition started at hockey games in the early 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-4) This is often followed by chants of "Spin your body!", and occasionally "Spin your tail!", with Goldy abiding and spinning the respective body parts. 1990s hockey games also sometimes featured Goldy sledding down the entirety of the [Mariucci Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M_Arena_at_Mariucci "3M Arena at Mariucci") staircase, nearly 30 rows. The tradition has been reigned in since then for safety concerns, but Goldy can still be found sledding and snowboarding from reduced heights.

The style of the gopher suit changed many times through the years, sometimes by chance, sometimes by design. Until the early 1970s, the head was narrow and pointy-nosed, reminiscent of the real animal. Then in 1972, Goldy suddenly grew chubby cheeks and a wider, forward-looking face, almost cherubic in appearance. The gopher of the 1970s and early 1980s was comparable in appearance to a teddy bear, a favorite of children and grandmothers. For a brief period in 1985, a fierce-looking “mega-rodent“ appeared, with a barrel chest, clown feet and sinister eyes. This look didn't last long, and Goldy soon again became a lovable, friendly character.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-5)

The students that portray Goldy maintain anonymity throughout their tenure. They are also recognized as student athletes due to their vigorous schedule and amount of work that goes into it.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3) They are considered a part of the "Spirit Squad" at the University of Minnesota, which encompasses the cheerleading and dance teams.

## Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design")]

Goldy’s first official design was made in the 1940s by sports merchandiser George Grooms, featuring a smiling "gopher" wearing a hat with the letter M on it.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-6) Grooms, while driving to the University of Minnesota from Iowa, stopped at a rest stop and sketched what he thought were gophers. He presented the drawing to U of M bookstore manager Harold Smith, who loved it. Only after the image was put into production did it become realized that the animal drawn was actually a chipmunk.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Chipmunk-7)

In the 1950s, Goldy's look became more animated. In the 1960s and 1970s, Goldy became more slim and simplistic, and was often drawn wearing sporting equipment. In 1979, the University hired Bill Stein to draw a new look for Goldy, which consisted of the mascot waving and wearing a shirt.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Gopher_State-8) Some commented that this drawing of Goldy wasn't fierce enough as a college mascot,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Chipmunk-7) and in 1985, a new version of Goldy was drawn by Steve Wanvig, who was asked by the University to make a more aggressive look. This variation of Goldy was a buff gopher with a fierce expression; depicted to be wearing a sweater and charging.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Gopher_State-8) Students who preferred the old design formed a group called Save Our Wimp, who championed for the previous drawing's more mild design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-9) Responding to the criticism, the University's athletics department asked Wanvig in 1986 to tone down Goldy, who was then drawn in the same style, but without huge muscles and with a friendlier expression. This version of Goldy has been the one used since.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-10)

### Capital One

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Capital One")]

Goldy was nominated to and made the 2004, 2007, and 2010 Capital One All-American Mascot Team. In 2007 Goldy finished second to Zippy from the [University of Akron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Akron "University of Akron").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-15)

## Goldy Gopher statue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Goldy Gopher statue")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg/250px-Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldy_Gopher_(Bronze_and_Granite,_2015).jpg)

The Goldy Gopher statue in front of Coffman Memorial Union

Due to the contributions from students, faculty, family, alumni, and friends, the University of Minnesota's Student Union was able to fund the creation of an all bronze statue of Goldy the Gopher. This was a controversial issue for some in the university community because of the rising costs of tuition and the university's concurrent appeals to the state legislature for a tuition freeze. The goal of the statue, located in the front of [Coffman Memorial Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffman_Memorial_Union "Coffman Memorial Union"), was to promote school spirit and start new traditions. The University of Minnesota Administration hopes the iconic symbol will help students interact with the spirit and new traditions involving Goldy the Gopher. The statue is 6 feet 3 inches (1.91 m) tall and made of bronze granite. Next to the statue is a solid granite "M" that is 63 inches in width, 24 Inches in depth, and 48 inches in height (160 x 61 x 122 cm). It was sculpted by [Nicholas Legeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Legeros "Nicholas Legeros"), who is a Minnesota graduate from the fine arts academy. He has sculpted many pieces for the Twin Cities Metro area. The total cost of the statue was $95,000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-16)

On Monday, September 23, 2013, the Goldy statue was unveiled during the homecoming kickoff at noon - which happened to be Goldy Gopher's birthday. Governor [Mark Dayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dayton "Mark Dayton") declared this day Goldy Gopher Day to create a new tradition for the students.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-17) Supposedly if someone was to rub Goldy's front teeth, it will bring them good luck.

**Goldy Gopher** is the mascot for the University of Minnesota and the associated sports teams, known as the [Golden Gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers "Minnesota Golden Gophers"), as well as a four-time UCA Mascot National Champion (2011, 2013, 2017, and 2018).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-1) During the year, Goldy makes over 1000 appearances and is at virtually all home games for University teams, usually wearing the appropriate sporting attire. The mascot is based on the [thirteen-lined ground squirrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen-lined_ground_squirrel "Thirteen-lined ground squirrel"), colloquially referred to as a “gopher” in Minnesota.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-2)

## Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Origins")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg/250px-Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gopher_State_Cartoon.jpg)

The 1857 political cartoon from which Minnesota derived its nickname, "The Gopher State".

[Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") became known as the "Gopher State" in 1857, the result of a political cartoon ridiculing the $5 million Railroad Loan which helped open up the West. The cartoon portrayed shifty railroad barons as [striped gophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen-lined_ground_squirrel "Thirteen-lined ground squirrel") pulling a railroad car carrying the Territorial Legislature toward the "Slough of Despond". The first U of M yearbook bearing the name "Gopher Annual" appeared in 1887.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3)

Minnesota's athletic teams became widely known as the "Gophers" by the 1920s, but it was not until 1934 that [Halsey Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halsey_Hall "Halsey Hall"), great Minnesota sportswriter and broadcaster, dubbed [Bernie Bierman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Bierman "Bernie Bierman")'s all-gold uniformed team "The Golden Gophers". Bierman had chosen the gold color because the football blended in with the uniforms.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3)

The embodiment of the Gopher mascot came to life in 1952 when University of Minnesota assistant bandmaster Jerome Glass bought a fuzzy wool gopher suit with a [papier-mâché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papier-m%C3%A2ch%C3%A9 "Papier-mâché") head and asked one of the band members to climb into it.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3) "Goldy" Gopher (the first name seems to have appeared sometime in the 1960s) became a fixture within the [University of Minnesota Marching Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota_Marching_Band "University of Minnesota Marching Band") and Pep Band, as each year a band member was chosen to don the suit for that season. Wherever these two bands performed, Goldy was there to glad-hand with the crowd, hug the little kids, and torment the cheerleaders.

During the early 1960s, Goldy was written into the football pre-game and halftime shows with a specific place to be. Limited visibility from within the suit made it difficult to see out, and any of the suit's wearers with glasses would fog up while trying to peer out the mouth hole, as the eyeholes were useless. One benefit during the cold games at [Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Stadium_(University_of_Minnesota) "Memorial Stadium (University of Minnesota)") in November was that Goldy Gopher was one of the few fans that stayed warm.

## Attitude and attire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Attitude and attire")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg/250px-Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldy_Gopher_Volleyball.jpg)

Goldy Gopher [snowboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowboarding "Snowboarding") down a staircase at a [women's volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers_women's_volleyball "Minnesota Golden Gophers women's volleyball") game

Each band member who was allowed the joy of being the Gopher developed an individual personality, a unique way of relating to the crowd. The mystique of Goldy Gopher became a tradition that absolutely prohibited removal of the head while in public, maintaining an illusion for the younger children that Goldy Gopher was a real live huggable animal.

From 1952 until 1990, the Gopher appearing at U of M sports events was a member of the Marching Band, and a symbiosis developed through the years that on more than one occasion kept Goldy out of trouble. With a propensity for attracting tail-pulling kids, Goldy relied on the band to save the gopher from their clutches. And when the opposing team's cheerleaders or band members managed to “kidnap” the unfortunate rodent (a [Big Ten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference") tradition), band members would come to the rescue.

In the late 1980s the U of M Athletic Department began to make use of Goldy at an ever-increasing number of events, and held University-wide tryouts to secure a number of students who could cover the busy schedule. The Athletic Department's Spirit Squad officially took charge of Goldy in 1992.

A signature move of Goldy's is head spinning, usually brought on by crowd chants of "Spin your head!", a tradition started at hockey games in the early 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-4) This is often followed by chants of "Spin your body!", and occasionally "Spin your tail!", with Goldy abiding and spinning the respective body parts. 1990s hockey games also sometimes featured Goldy sledding down the entirety of the [Mariucci Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3M_Arena_at_Mariucci "3M Arena at Mariucci") staircase, nearly 30 rows. The tradition has been reigned in since then for safety concerns, but Goldy can still be found sledding and snowboarding from reduced heights.

The style of the gopher suit changed many times through the years, sometimes by chance, sometimes by design. Until the early 1970s, the head was narrow and pointy-nosed, reminiscent of the real animal. Then in 1972, Goldy suddenly grew chubby cheeks and a wider, forward-looking face, almost cherubic in appearance. The gopher of the 1970s and early 1980s was comparable in appearance to a teddy bear, a favorite of children and grandmothers. For a brief period in 1985, a fierce-looking “mega-rodent“ appeared, with a barrel chest, clown feet and sinister eyes. This look didn't last long, and Goldy soon again became a lovable, friendly character.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-5)

The students that portray Goldy maintain anonymity throughout their tenure. They are also recognized as student athletes due to their vigorous schedule and amount of work that goes into it.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Goldy-3) They are considered a part of the "Spirit Squad" at the University of Minnesota, which encompasses the cheerleading and dance teams.

## Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design")]

Goldy’s first official design was made in the 1940s by sports merchandiser George Grooms, featuring a smiling "gopher" wearing a hat with the letter M on it.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-6) Grooms, while driving to the University of Minnesota from Iowa, stopped at a rest stop and sketched what he thought were gophers. He presented the drawing to U of M bookstore manager Harold Smith, who loved it. Only after the image was put into production did it become realized that the animal drawn was actually a chipmunk.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Chipmunk-7)

In the 1950s, Goldy's look became more animated. In the 1960s and 1970s, Goldy became more slim and simplistic, and was often drawn wearing sporting equipment. In 1979, the University hired Bill Stein to draw a new look for Goldy, which consisted of the mascot waving and wearing a shirt.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Gopher_State-8) Some commented that this drawing of Goldy wasn't fierce enough as a college mascot,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Chipmunk-7) and in 1985, a new version of Goldy was drawn by Steve Wanvig, who was asked by the University to make a more aggressive look. This variation of Goldy was a buff gopher with a fierce expression; depicted to be wearing a sweater and charging.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-Gopher_State-8) Students who preferred the old design formed a group called Save Our Wimp, who championed for the previous drawing's more mild design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-9) Responding to the criticism, the University's athletics department asked Wanvig in 1986 to tone down Goldy, who was then drawn in the same style, but without huge muscles and with a friendlier expression. This version of Goldy has been the one used since.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-10)

### Capital One

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Capital One")]

Goldy was nominated to and made the 2004, 2007, and 2010 Capital One All-American Mascot Team. In 2007 Goldy finished second to Zippy from the [University of Akron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Akron "University of Akron").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-15)

## Goldy Gopher statue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goldy_Gopher&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Goldy Gopher statue")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg/250px-Goldy_Gopher_%28Bronze_and_Granite%2C_2015%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldy_Gopher_(Bronze_and_Granite,_2015).jpg)

The Goldy Gopher statue in front of Coffman Memorial Union

Due to the contributions from students, faculty, family, alumni, and friends, the University of Minnesota's Student Union was able to fund the creation of an all bronze statue of Goldy the Gopher. This was a controversial issue for some in the university community because of the rising costs of tuition and the university's concurrent appeals to the state legislature for a tuition freeze. The goal of the statue, located in the front of [Coffman Memorial Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffman_Memorial_Union "Coffman Memorial Union"), was to promote school spirit and start new traditions. The University of Minnesota Administration hopes the iconic symbol will help students interact with the spirit and new traditions involving Goldy the Gopher. The statue is 6 feet 3 inches (1.91 m) tall and made of bronze granite. Next to the statue is a solid granite "M" that is 63 inches in width, 24 Inches in depth, and 48 inches in height (160 x 61 x 122 cm). It was sculpted by [Nicholas Legeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Legeros "Nicholas Legeros"), who is a Minnesota graduate from the fine arts academy. He has sculpted many pieces for the Twin Cities Metro area. The total cost of the statue was $95,000.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-16)

On Monday, September 23, 2013, the Goldy statue was unveiled during the homecoming kickoff at noon - which happened to be Goldy Gopher's birthday. Governor [Mark Dayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dayton "Mark Dayton") declared this day Goldy Gopher Day to create a new tradition for the students.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldy_Gopher#cite_note-17) Supposedly if someone was to rub Goldy's front teeth, it will bring them good luck.

**Mount Whitney** ([Paiute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Paiute_language "Northern Paiute language"): _Tumanguya_) is a mountain in California's [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada "Sierra Nevada") range, and is the highest point in the [contiguous United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguous_United_States "Contiguous United States"), with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs-1) It is located in [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_California "Eastern California")–[Central California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_California "Central California") along the border of [Inyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_County,_California "Inyo County, California") and [Tulare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulare_County,_California "Tulare County, California") counties. The mountain's west slope is in [Sequoia National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_National_Park "Sequoia National Park") and the summit is the southern terminus of the [John Muir Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trail "John Muir Trail"), which runs 211.9 mi (341.0 km) from [Happy Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Isles "Happy Isles") in [Yosemite Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Valley "Yosemite Valley").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-YOSE-6) The eastern slopes are in [Inyo National Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_National_Forest "Inyo National Forest") in [Inyo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_County "Inyo County"). Mount Whitney is ranked 18th by [topographic isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_isolation "Topographic isolation") and 81st by [prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_peaks_by_prominence "List of peaks by prominence") on Earth. It is the tallest mountain in the United States outside of [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska").

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/A347%2C_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney%2C_California%2C_USA%2C_2011.JPG/250px-A347%2C_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney%2C_California%2C_USA%2C_2011.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A347,_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney,_California,_USA,_2011.JPG)

[Sky pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemonium_eximium "Polemonium eximium") blooming on ridge just below summit

Mount Whitney's summit is on the [Sierra Crest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Crest "Sierra Crest") and the [Great Basin Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin_Divide "Great Basin Divide"). It lies near many of the [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(U.S.) "Sierra Nevada (U.S.)")'s highest peaks.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Sierra-7) The peak rises dramatically above the [Owens Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_Valley "Owens Valley"), sitting 10,778 feet (3,285 m) or just over 2 mi (3.2 km) above the town of [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California")15 mi (24 km) to the east, in the Owens Valley.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Sierra-7) It rises more gradually on the west side, lying only about 3,000 feet (914 m) above the John Muir Trail at Guitar Lake.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Guitar-8)

The mountain is partially dome-shaped, with its famously jagged ridges extending to the sides.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-backpacker-9) Mount Whitney is above the [tree line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_line "Tree line") and has an [alpine climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_climate "Alpine climate") and [ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_tundra "Alpine tundra").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ABC-10) Very few plants grow near the summit: one example is the [sky pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemonium_eximium "Polemonium eximium"), a [cushion plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushion_plant "Cushion plant") that grows low to the ground.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11) The only animals are transient, such as the butterfly _[Parnassius phoebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parnassius\_phoebus "Parnassius phoebus")_ and the [gray-crowned rosy finch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey-crowned_rosy_finch "Grey-crowned rosy finch").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11)

### Hydrology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Hydrology")]

The mountain is the highest point on the [Great Basin Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin_Divide "Great Basin Divide"). Waterways on the peak's west side flow into Whitney Creek, which flows into the [Kern River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kern_River "Kern River"). The Kern River terminates at [Bakersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakersfield,_California "Bakersfield, California") in the [Tulare Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulare_Lake "Tulare Lake"), the southern part of the [San Joaquin Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_Valley "San Joaquin Valley"). Today, the water in the Tulare Basin is largely diverted for agriculture. Historically, during very wet years, water overflowed from the Tulare Basin into the [San Joaquin River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_River "San Joaquin River"), which flows to the Pacific Ocean.

From the east, water from Mount Whitney flows to Lone Pine Creek, where most of the water is diverted into the [Los Angeles Aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Aqueduct "Los Angeles Aqueduct") via a [sluice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluice "Sluice"). Some water in the creek is allowed to continue on its natural course, joining the [Owens River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_River "Owens River"), which terminates at [Owens Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_Lake "Owens Lake"), an [endorheic lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorheic_basin#Endorheic_lakes "Endorheic basin") of the [Great Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin "Great Basin").

### Elevation measurements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Elevation measurements")]

The estimated elevation of Mount Whitney's summit has changed over the years. The technology of elevation measurement has become more refined and, more importantly, the vertical coordinate system has changed. The peak was commonly said to be at 14,494 ft (4,418 m) and this is the elevation stamped on the [USGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") brass [benchmark disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benchmark_(surveying) "Benchmark (surveying)") on the summit. An older plaque on the summit (sheet metal with black lettering on white enamel) reads "elevation 14,496.811 feet", but this was estimated using the older [vertical datum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodetic_system "Geodetic system") ([NGVD29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Level_Datum_of_1929 "Sea Level Datum of 1929")) from 1929. Since then the shape of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") (the [geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid "Geoid")) has been estimated more accurately. Using a new vertical datum established in 1988 ([NAVD88](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Vertical_Datum_of_1988 "North American Vertical Datum of 1988")) the benchmark is now estimated to be 14,504 ft (4,421 m).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs-1)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs_hcm-12)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate")]

Mount Whitney has an [alpine tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_climate "Polar climate") (_ET_) under the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"). Summer temperatures are highly variable, ranging from below freezing (32°F (0°C)) to highs near 80°F (27°C) during extreme heat waves in the Owens Valley.

Based on the range from the highest average high of 25.7°F (−3.5°C) to the lowest average low of 4.2°F (−15.4°C) for winter temperatures in the table (December to March), every 1 inch (25 mm) of liquid precipitation equates to approximately 15–40 inches (380–1,020 mm) of snow, with lower temperatures producing the greater snow depths.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-13)

There is no weather station at the summit, but this climate table contains [interpolated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpolation "Interpolation") data for an area below the summit.
