## Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geology")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg/250px-Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg)

Schematic of Sierra Nevada [fault block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_block "Fault block")

Whitney's eastern slope is far steeper than its western because the Sierra Nevada is the result of a [fault block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_block "Fault block") anchored below the surface to the west and slowly rising on the east.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-usfs_sn-15)

The rise is caused by a [fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)") system that runs along the Sierra's eastern base, below Mount Whitney. The [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") that forms Whitney, part of the [Sierra Nevada Batholith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Batholith "Sierra Nevada Batholith"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-mcphee-16) is the same as that of the [Alabama Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_Hills "Alabama Hills") thousands of feet lower and to the east.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11) The raising of Whitney (and the downdrop of the Owens Valley) is due to the same geological forces that cause the [Basin and Range Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basin_and_Range_Province "Basin and Range Province"): the crust of much of the intermontane west is slowly being stretched.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nps-17)

In [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") time, masses of molten rock that originated from [subduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") rose underneath what is now Whitney and solidified underground to form large expanses of granite.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-mcphee-16) In the last 2 to 10 million years, the Sierra was pushed up, enabling glacial and river erosion to strip the upper layers of softer rock to reveal the resistant granite that makes up Mount Whitney.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-stephen-18)

About 50 to 60 million years ago, during the [Cenozoic Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenozoic "Cenozoic"), tectonic uplifts began to form the present Sierra range. These uplifts tilted the region towards the southwest causing rivers to form. As the land continued to rise, rivers and streams cut deeper and carved out valleys.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-19)

## Exploration history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Exploration history")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg/250px-Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg)

Mount Whitney as seen from [Mount Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Langley "Mount Langley")

In July 1864, the members of the [California Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Geological_Survey "California Geological Survey") named the peak, the contiguous United States' highest summit, after [Josiah Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Whitney "Josiah Whitney"), the state geologist of [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and sponsor of the survey.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Farquhar-5) During the same expedition, geologist [Clarence King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_King "Clarence King") attempted to climb Whitney from its west side, but stopped just short. In 1871, King returned to climb what he believed to be Whitney, but having taken a different approach, he actually summited nearby [Mount Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Langley "Mount Langley"). Upon learning of his mistake in 1873, King finally completed his own first ascent of Whitney, but did so a month too late to be first.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-King-20) On August 18, 1873, Charles Begole, A. H. Johnson, and John Lucas, all of nearby [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California"), had become the first to reach the summit. As they climbed the mountain during a fishing trip to nearby Kern Canyon, they called the mountain Fisherman's Peak.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Farquhar-5)

In 1881, [Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Astrophysical_Observatory "Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory") founder [Samuel Pierpont Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pierpont_Langley "Samuel Pierpont Langley") remained on the summit for some time, making daily observations of the solar heat.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ea-21) Accompanying Langley in 1881 was another party consisting of Judge William B. Wallace of Visalia, W. A. Wright and Reverend Frederick Wales.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-seq-22) In his memoirs,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-paiute-23) Wallace wrote, "The [Pi Ute [Paiute]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Paiute "Northern Paiute") Indians called Mount Whitney _Too-man-i-goo-yah_, which means 'the very old man.' They believe that the Great Spirit who presides over the destiny of their people once had his home in that mountain." The spelling _Too-man-i-goo-yah_ is a transliteration from the indigenous Paiute [Mono language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mono_language_(California) "Mono language (California)"). Another variation is _Too-man-go-yah._[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-14ers-24)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg/250px-Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg)

The [Smithsonian Institution Shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Shelter "Smithsonian Institution Shelter") on Whitney's summit

In 1891, the [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey")'s Board on Geographic Names decided to recognize the name Mount Whitney. Despite losing out on their preferred name, Lone Pine residents financed a trail to the summit, engineered by Gustave Marsh, and completed on July 22, 1904. Four days later, the new trail enabled the first recorded death on Whitney. Having hiked the trail, [U.S. Bureau of Fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service "United States Fish and Wildlife Service") employee Byrd Surby was struck and killed by lightning while eating lunch on the summit. In response, Marsh began work on the stone hut that became the [Smithsonian Institution Shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Shelter "Smithsonian Institution Shelter"), completing it in 1909.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-LPC-25)

Although Gustave Marsh is often credited for constructing the first trail to the peak of Mount Whitney, a lesser known trail to the peak was created by the [Buffalo Soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Soldier "Buffalo Soldier"), the first all-black Army regiments in peacetime,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-26) a year prior in 1903.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-:0-27) In addition to creating trails, the Buffalo Soldiers fought fires, built fences, and kept illegal grazers away.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-28)[Charles Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Young_(United_States_Army_officer) "Charles Young (United States Army officer)"), a Buffalo Soldier officer, served as the acting military superintendent of [Sequoia National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_National_Park "Sequoia National Park") (where Mount Whitney is located) in 1903.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-:0-27) He is considered the first African-American superintendent of a national park.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-29) The Buffalo soldiers also built a wagon road into the [Giant Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Forest "Giant Forest") which later became [Generals Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generals_Highway "Generals Highway") and is the modern day route for automobiles driving to Mount Whitney.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nationalgeographic.com-30)

A movement began after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") to rename the mountain for [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-gnis-31) but the name Mount Whitney persisted.

## Climbing routes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Climbing routes")]

### Trails

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Trails")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg/250px-Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg)

The [Mount Whitney Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Whitney_Trail "Mount Whitney Trail")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Whitney-icy-trail.jpg/250px-Whitney-icy-trail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitney-icy-trail.jpg)

1962 before railings, opposite view, treacherous.

The most popular route to the summit is by way of the [Mount Whitney Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Whitney_Trail "Mount Whitney Trail"), which starts at [Whitney Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Portal "Whitney Portal") and incorporates the original path to the summit built by the [Buffalo Soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Soldier "Buffalo Soldier"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nationalgeographic.com-30) at an elevation of 8,360 ft (2,548 m), 13 mi (21 km) west of the town of [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California"). The hike is about 22 mi (35 km) round trip with an elevation gain of over 6,100 ft (1,859 m). Permits are required year-round, and to prevent overuse the [Forest Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Forest_Service "United States Forest Service") issues a limited number of permits between May 1 and November 1.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-32) It holds an annual lottery for hiking and backpacking permits on the trail. Applications are accepted from February 1 through March 15. Any permits left over after the lottery is completed typically go on sale April 1. Most hikers plan to stay one or two nights, camping along the route.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-33) Those in good physical condition sometimes attempt to reach the summit and return to Whitney Portal in one day. A one-day hike requires a day-use permit that prohibits the use of overnight camping gear (sleeping bag and tent). Day hikers often leave Whitney Portal before sunrise and hike for 12 to 18 hours.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-dayhiker-34)

Longer approaches to Whitney arrive at its west side, connecting to the Mount Whitney Trail near the summit by way of the [John Muir Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trail "John Muir Trail") (Also referred to as _Nüümü Poyo_, an Indigenous Paiute name meaning "People's Trail"[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-35)).

### Scrambles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Scrambles")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg/250px-Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg)

Aerial view of the Mount Whitney [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif") and the steep eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, from the north

The Mountaineer's Route, a gully on the north side of the east face first climbed by [John Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir "John Muir"), is considered a [scramble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrambling "Scrambling"), [class 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Decimal_System "Yosemite Decimal System") ([PD+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_(climbing)#International_French_adjectival_system_(IFAS) "Grade (climbing)")).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Secor-36) The fastest recorded time up this route to the summit and back to the portal is 3 hours 10 minutes, by Jason Lakey of [Bishop, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop,_California "Bishop, California").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-rockice-37)

### Technical climbs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Technical climbs")]

The steep eastern side of the mountain offers a variety of climbing challenges. The [East Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Face_(Mount_Whitney) "East Face (Mount Whitney)") route, first climbed in 1931, is one of the _[Fifty Classic Climbs of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifty\_Classic\_Climbs\_of\_North\_America "Fifty Classic Climbs of North America")_[routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_route "Climbing route"), and involves technical [free climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_climbing "Free climbing") ([class 5.7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Decimal_System "Yosemite Decimal System")) but is mostly class 4. Other routes range up to grade 5.10d.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Secor-36)

South of the main summit is a series of minor summits that are completely inconspicuous from the west but appear as a series of "needles" from the east. The routes on these include some of the finest big-wall climbing in the high Sierra. Two of the needles were named after participants in an 1880 scientific expedition to the mountain: Keeler Needle for [James Keeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Edward_Keeler "James Edward Keeler"), and Day Needle for William Cathcart Day. The latter was renamed in 1990 by Congressional act as Crooks Peak after [Hulda Crooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulda_Crooks "Hulda Crooks"), who hiked up Mount Whitney every year until well into her nineties.

**Mount Whitney** ([Paiute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Paiute_language "Northern Paiute language"): _Tumanguya_) is a mountain in California's [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada "Sierra Nevada") range, and is the highest point in the [contiguous United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguous_United_States "Contiguous United States"), with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs-1) It is located in [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_California "Eastern California")–[Central California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_California "Central California") along the border of [Inyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_County,_California "Inyo County, California") and [Tulare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulare_County,_California "Tulare County, California") counties. The mountain's west slope is in [Sequoia National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_National_Park "Sequoia National Park") and the summit is the southern terminus of the [John Muir Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trail "John Muir Trail"), which runs 211.9 mi (341.0 km) from [Happy Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Isles "Happy Isles") in [Yosemite Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Valley "Yosemite Valley").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-YOSE-6) The eastern slopes are in [Inyo National Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_National_Forest "Inyo National Forest") in [Inyo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inyo_County "Inyo County"). Mount Whitney is ranked 18th by [topographic isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_isolation "Topographic isolation") and 81st by [prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_peaks_by_prominence "List of peaks by prominence") on Earth. It is the tallest mountain in the United States outside of [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska").

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/A347%2C_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney%2C_California%2C_USA%2C_2011.JPG/250px-A347%2C_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney%2C_California%2C_USA%2C_2011.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A347,_Skypilot_near_summit_of_Mount_Whitney,_California,_USA,_2011.JPG)

[Sky pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemonium_eximium "Polemonium eximium") blooming on ridge just below summit

Mount Whitney's summit is on the [Sierra Crest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Crest "Sierra Crest") and the [Great Basin Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin_Divide "Great Basin Divide"). It lies near many of the [Sierra Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_(U.S.) "Sierra Nevada (U.S.)")'s highest peaks.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Sierra-7) The peak rises dramatically above the [Owens Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_Valley "Owens Valley"), sitting 10,778 feet (3,285 m) or just over 2 mi (3.2 km) above the town of [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California")15 mi (24 km) to the east, in the Owens Valley.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Sierra-7) It rises more gradually on the west side, lying only about 3,000 feet (914 m) above the John Muir Trail at Guitar Lake.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Guitar-8)

The mountain is partially dome-shaped, with its famously jagged ridges extending to the sides.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-backpacker-9) Mount Whitney is above the [tree line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_line "Tree line") and has an [alpine climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_climate "Alpine climate") and [ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_tundra "Alpine tundra").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ABC-10) Very few plants grow near the summit: one example is the [sky pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemonium_eximium "Polemonium eximium"), a [cushion plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushion_plant "Cushion plant") that grows low to the ground.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11) The only animals are transient, such as the butterfly _[Parnassius phoebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parnassius\_phoebus "Parnassius phoebus")_ and the [gray-crowned rosy finch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey-crowned_rosy_finch "Grey-crowned rosy finch").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11)

### Hydrology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Hydrology")]

The mountain is the highest point on the [Great Basin Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin_Divide "Great Basin Divide"). Waterways on the peak's west side flow into Whitney Creek, which flows into the [Kern River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kern_River "Kern River"). The Kern River terminates at [Bakersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakersfield,_California "Bakersfield, California") in the [Tulare Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulare_Lake "Tulare Lake"), the southern part of the [San Joaquin Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_Valley "San Joaquin Valley"). Today, the water in the Tulare Basin is largely diverted for agriculture. Historically, during very wet years, water overflowed from the Tulare Basin into the [San Joaquin River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Joaquin_River "San Joaquin River"), which flows to the Pacific Ocean.

From the east, water from Mount Whitney flows to Lone Pine Creek, where most of the water is diverted into the [Los Angeles Aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Aqueduct "Los Angeles Aqueduct") via a [sluice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluice "Sluice"). Some water in the creek is allowed to continue on its natural course, joining the [Owens River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_River "Owens River"), which terminates at [Owens Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owens_Lake "Owens Lake"), an [endorheic lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorheic_basin#Endorheic_lakes "Endorheic basin") of the [Great Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin "Great Basin").

### Elevation measurements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Elevation measurements")]

The estimated elevation of Mount Whitney's summit has changed over the years. The technology of elevation measurement has become more refined and, more importantly, the vertical coordinate system has changed. The peak was commonly said to be at 14,494 ft (4,418 m) and this is the elevation stamped on the [USGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") brass [benchmark disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benchmark_(surveying) "Benchmark (surveying)") on the summit. An older plaque on the summit (sheet metal with black lettering on white enamel) reads "elevation 14,496.811 feet", but this was estimated using the older [vertical datum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodetic_system "Geodetic system") ([NGVD29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Level_Datum_of_1929 "Sea Level Datum of 1929")) from 1929. Since then the shape of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth") (the [geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid "Geoid")) has been estimated more accurately. Using a new vertical datum established in 1988 ([NAVD88](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Vertical_Datum_of_1988 "North American Vertical Datum of 1988")) the benchmark is now estimated to be 14,504 ft (4,421 m).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs-1)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ngs_hcm-12)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate")]

Mount Whitney has an [alpine tundra climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_climate "Polar climate") (_ET_) under the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"). Summer temperatures are highly variable, ranging from below freezing (32°F (0°C)) to highs near 80°F (27°C) during extreme heat waves in the Owens Valley.

Based on the range from the highest average high of 25.7°F (−3.5°C) to the lowest average low of 4.2°F (−15.4°C) for winter temperatures in the table (December to March), every 1 inch (25 mm) of liquid precipitation equates to approximately 15–40 inches (380–1,020 mm) of snow, with lower temperatures producing the greater snow depths.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-13)

There is no weather station at the summit, but this climate table contains [interpolated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpolation "Interpolation") data for an area below the summit.

## Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geology")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg/250px-Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sierra_nevada_schematic.svg)

Schematic of Sierra Nevada [fault block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_block "Fault block")

Whitney's eastern slope is far steeper than its western because the Sierra Nevada is the result of a [fault block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_block "Fault block") anchored below the surface to the west and slowly rising on the east.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-usfs_sn-15)

The rise is caused by a [fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)") system that runs along the Sierra's eastern base, below Mount Whitney. The [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") that forms Whitney, part of the [Sierra Nevada Batholith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Batholith "Sierra Nevada Batholith"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-mcphee-16) is the same as that of the [Alabama Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_Hills "Alabama Hills") thousands of feet lower and to the east.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Schoenherr-11) The raising of Whitney (and the downdrop of the Owens Valley) is due to the same geological forces that cause the [Basin and Range Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basin_and_Range_Province "Basin and Range Province"): the crust of much of the intermontane west is slowly being stretched.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nps-17)

In [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") time, masses of molten rock that originated from [subduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") rose underneath what is now Whitney and solidified underground to form large expanses of granite.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-mcphee-16) In the last 2 to 10 million years, the Sierra was pushed up, enabling glacial and river erosion to strip the upper layers of softer rock to reveal the resistant granite that makes up Mount Whitney.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-stephen-18)

About 50 to 60 million years ago, during the [Cenozoic Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenozoic "Cenozoic"), tectonic uplifts began to form the present Sierra range. These uplifts tilted the region towards the southwest causing rivers to form. As the land continued to rise, rivers and streams cut deeper and carved out valleys.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-19)

## Exploration history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Exploration history")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg/250px-Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Whitney_from_south.jpg)

Mount Whitney as seen from [Mount Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Langley "Mount Langley")

In July 1864, the members of the [California Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Geological_Survey "California Geological Survey") named the peak, the contiguous United States' highest summit, after [Josiah Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Whitney "Josiah Whitney"), the state geologist of [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") and sponsor of the survey.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Farquhar-5) During the same expedition, geologist [Clarence King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_King "Clarence King") attempted to climb Whitney from its west side, but stopped just short. In 1871, King returned to climb what he believed to be Whitney, but having taken a different approach, he actually summited nearby [Mount Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Langley "Mount Langley"). Upon learning of his mistake in 1873, King finally completed his own first ascent of Whitney, but did so a month too late to be first.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-King-20) On August 18, 1873, Charles Begole, A. H. Johnson, and John Lucas, all of nearby [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California"), had become the first to reach the summit. As they climbed the mountain during a fishing trip to nearby Kern Canyon, they called the mountain Fisherman's Peak.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Farquhar-5)

In 1881, [Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Astrophysical_Observatory "Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory") founder [Samuel Pierpont Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pierpont_Langley "Samuel Pierpont Langley") remained on the summit for some time, making daily observations of the solar heat.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-ea-21) Accompanying Langley in 1881 was another party consisting of Judge William B. Wallace of Visalia, W. A. Wright and Reverend Frederick Wales.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-seq-22) In his memoirs,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-paiute-23) Wallace wrote, "The [Pi Ute [Paiute]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Paiute "Northern Paiute") Indians called Mount Whitney _Too-man-i-goo-yah_, which means 'the very old man.' They believe that the Great Spirit who presides over the destiny of their people once had his home in that mountain." The spelling _Too-man-i-goo-yah_ is a transliteration from the indigenous Paiute [Mono language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mono_language_(California) "Mono language (California)"). Another variation is _Too-man-go-yah._[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-14ers-24)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg/250px-Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smithsonian_Hut_Whitney.jpg)

The [Smithsonian Institution Shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Shelter "Smithsonian Institution Shelter") on Whitney's summit

In 1891, the [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey")'s Board on Geographic Names decided to recognize the name Mount Whitney. Despite losing out on their preferred name, Lone Pine residents financed a trail to the summit, engineered by Gustave Marsh, and completed on July 22, 1904. Four days later, the new trail enabled the first recorded death on Whitney. Having hiked the trail, [U.S. Bureau of Fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service "United States Fish and Wildlife Service") employee Byrd Surby was struck and killed by lightning while eating lunch on the summit. In response, Marsh began work on the stone hut that became the [Smithsonian Institution Shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution_Shelter "Smithsonian Institution Shelter"), completing it in 1909.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-LPC-25)

Although Gustave Marsh is often credited for constructing the first trail to the peak of Mount Whitney, a lesser known trail to the peak was created by the [Buffalo Soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Soldier "Buffalo Soldier"), the first all-black Army regiments in peacetime,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-26) a year prior in 1903.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-:0-27) In addition to creating trails, the Buffalo Soldiers fought fires, built fences, and kept illegal grazers away.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-28)[Charles Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Young_(United_States_Army_officer) "Charles Young (United States Army officer)"), a Buffalo Soldier officer, served as the acting military superintendent of [Sequoia National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoia_National_Park "Sequoia National Park") (where Mount Whitney is located) in 1903.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-:0-27) He is considered the first African-American superintendent of a national park.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-29) The Buffalo soldiers also built a wagon road into the [Giant Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Forest "Giant Forest") which later became [Generals Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generals_Highway "Generals Highway") and is the modern day route for automobiles driving to Mount Whitney.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nationalgeographic.com-30)

A movement began after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") to rename the mountain for [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-gnis-31) but the name Mount Whitney persisted.

## Climbing routes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Climbing routes")]

### Trails

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Trails")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg/250px-Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitney_Trail_Switchbacks.jpg)

The [Mount Whitney Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Whitney_Trail "Mount Whitney Trail")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Whitney-icy-trail.jpg/250px-Whitney-icy-trail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitney-icy-trail.jpg)

1962 before railings, opposite view, treacherous.

The most popular route to the summit is by way of the [Mount Whitney Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Whitney_Trail "Mount Whitney Trail"), which starts at [Whitney Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Portal "Whitney Portal") and incorporates the original path to the summit built by the [Buffalo Soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Soldier "Buffalo Soldier"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-nationalgeographic.com-30) at an elevation of 8,360 ft (2,548 m), 13 mi (21 km) west of the town of [Lone Pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Pine,_California "Lone Pine, California"). The hike is about 22 mi (35 km) round trip with an elevation gain of over 6,100 ft (1,859 m). Permits are required year-round, and to prevent overuse the [Forest Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Forest_Service "United States Forest Service") issues a limited number of permits between May 1 and November 1.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-32) It holds an annual lottery for hiking and backpacking permits on the trail. Applications are accepted from February 1 through March 15. Any permits left over after the lottery is completed typically go on sale April 1. Most hikers plan to stay one or two nights, camping along the route.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-33) Those in good physical condition sometimes attempt to reach the summit and return to Whitney Portal in one day. A one-day hike requires a day-use permit that prohibits the use of overnight camping gear (sleeping bag and tent). Day hikers often leave Whitney Portal before sunrise and hike for 12 to 18 hours.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-dayhiker-34)

Longer approaches to Whitney arrive at its west side, connecting to the Mount Whitney Trail near the summit by way of the [John Muir Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trail "John Muir Trail") (Also referred to as _Nüümü Poyo_, an Indigenous Paiute name meaning "People's Trail"[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-35)).

### Scrambles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Scrambles")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg/250px-Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mt._Whitney_and_south-eastern_Sierra_Nevada_aerial.jpg)

Aerial view of the Mount Whitney [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif") and the steep eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, from the north

The Mountaineer's Route, a gully on the north side of the east face first climbed by [John Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir "John Muir"), is considered a [scramble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrambling "Scrambling"), [class 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Decimal_System "Yosemite Decimal System") ([PD+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_(climbing)#International_French_adjectival_system_(IFAS) "Grade (climbing)")).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Secor-36) The fastest recorded time up this route to the summit and back to the portal is 3 hours 10 minutes, by Jason Lakey of [Bishop, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop,_California "Bishop, California").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-rockice-37)

### Technical climbs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mount_Whitney&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Technical climbs")]

The steep eastern side of the mountain offers a variety of climbing challenges. The [East Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Face_(Mount_Whitney) "East Face (Mount Whitney)") route, first climbed in 1931, is one of the _[Fifty Classic Climbs of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifty\_Classic\_Climbs\_of\_North\_America "Fifty Classic Climbs of North America")_[routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_route "Climbing route"), and involves technical [free climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_climbing "Free climbing") ([class 5.7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yosemite_Decimal_System "Yosemite Decimal System")) but is mostly class 4. Other routes range up to grade 5.10d.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Whitney#cite_note-Secor-36)

South of the main summit is a series of minor summits that are completely inconspicuous from the west but appear as a series of "needles" from the east. The routes on these include some of the finest big-wall climbing in the high Sierra. Two of the needles were named after participants in an 1880 scientific expedition to the mountain: Keeler Needle for [James Keeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Edward_Keeler "James Edward Keeler"), and Day Needle for William Cathcart Day. The latter was renamed in 1990 by Congressional act as Crooks Peak after [Hulda Crooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulda_Crooks "Hulda Crooks"), who hiked up Mount Whitney every year until well into her nineties.
