Main article: [Pearl Milling Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Milling_Company "Pearl Milling Company")

In 1888, _[St. Joseph Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St.\_Joseph\_Gazette "St. Joseph Gazette")_ editor [Chris L. Rutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_L._Rutt "Chris L. Rutt") and his friend Charles G. Underwood bought a small [flour mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gristmill "Gristmill") at 214 North 2nd St. in [St. Joseph, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph,_Missouri "St. Joseph, Missouri").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-11) Rutt and Underwood's "Pearl Milling Company" produced a range of milled products (such as [wheat flour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheat_flour "Wheat flour") and [cornmeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornmeal "Cornmeal")) using a pearl-milling process.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-12) Facing a glutted flour market, after a year of experimentation, they began selling their excess flour in paper bags with the generic label "Self-Rising Pancake Flour" (later dubbed "the first [ready-mix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baking_mix "Baking mix")").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-history_2007-08-23-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13)

### Branding and trademark

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Branding and trademark")]

To distinguish their pancake mix, in late 1889, Rutt appropriated the _Aunt Jemima_ name and image from [lithographed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") posters seen at a [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") house in St. Joseph, Missouri.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13) At the 1893 [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), the company set up a pancake-cooking display next to the "world's largest flour barrel" (twenty-four feet high). [Nancy Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Green "Nancy Green"), a former slave from [Montgomery County, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_County,_Kentucky "Montgomery County, Kentucky"), portrayed the character and cooked pancakes, sang songs, and promoted the product.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_2008-15)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-16)

In 1915, the well known Aunt Jemima brand was the basis for a trademark law ruling that set a new precedent. Previously, [United States trademark law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_trademark_law "United States trademark law") had protected against infringement by other sellers of the same product, but, under the "Aunt Jemima Doctrine", the seller of pancake mix was also protected against infringement by an unrelated seller of a different but related product: pancake syrup.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-17) Aunt Jemima became one of the longest continually running logos and trademarks in the history of American advertising.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2015-06-24-18)

### Logo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Logo")]

The earliest advertising was based upon a vaudeville parody, and it remained a [caricature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caricature "Caricature") for many years.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13)

Quaker Oats commissioned [Haddon Sundblom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haddon_Sundblom "Haddon Sundblom"), a nationally known commercial artist, to paint a portrait of an obese actress named Anna Robinson, and the Aunt Jemima package was redesigned around the new likeness.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)

James J. Jaffee, a freelance artist from the Bronx, New York, also designed one of the images of Aunt Jemima used by Quaker Oats to market the product into the mid-20th century.

Just as the formula for the mix changed several times over the years, so did the Aunt Jemima image. In 1968, the face of Aunt Jemima became a composited creation. She was slimmed down from her previous appearance, depicting a more "svelte" look, wearing a white collar and a geometric print "headband" still resembling her previous kerchief.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-ChicTrib-89-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-AP-89-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Ingrano_2019-21)

In 1989, marking the 100th anniversary of the brand, her image was again updated, with all head-covering removed, revealing wavy, gray-streaked hair, gold-trimmed pearl earrings, and replacing her plain white collar with lace. At the time, the revised image was described as a move towards a more "sophisticated" depiction, with Quaker marketing the change as giving her "a more contemporary look", which remained on the products until early 2021.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-ChicTrib-89-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-AP-89-20)

### Rebranding of 2020–2021

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rebranding of 2020–2021")]

On June 17, 2020, Quaker Oats announced that the Aunt Jemima brand would be discontinued and replaced with a new name and image "to make progress toward racial equality".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-nbc_2020-06-17-4)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-cnn_2020-06-17-22) The image was removed from packaging in fall 2020, while the name change was said to be planned for a later date.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-forbes_2020-06-17-24)

Within one day of the June 2020 announcement, other similarly motivated rebrandings and reviews of brand marketing were also announced, including for [Uncle Ben's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Ben's "Uncle Ben's") rice (which was renamed [Ben's Original](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben's_Original "Ben's Original")), the [Mrs. Butterworth's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs._Butterworth's "Mrs. Butterworth's") pancake syrup brand and bottle shape, and the "[Rastus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastus "Rastus")" black-chef logo used by [Cream of Wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_of_Wheat "Cream of Wheat").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-cnn_2021-02-06-7)

Descendants of Aunt Jemima models [Lillian Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Richard "Lillian Richard") and [Anna Short Harrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Short_Harrington "Anna Short Harrington") objected to the change. Vera Harris, a family historian for Richard's family, said "I wish we would take a breath and not just get rid of everything. Because good or bad, it is our history."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-25) Harris further stated that "Erasing my Aunt Lillian Richard would erase a part of history."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-26) Harrington's great-grandson Larnell Evans said "This is an injustice for me and my family. This is part of my history." Evans had previously lost a [lawsuit against Quaker Oats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Short_Harrington#Lawsuit "Anna Short Harrington") (and others) for billions of dollars in 2015.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-27)

On February 9, 2021, [PepsiCo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PepsiCo "PepsiCo") announced that the replacement brand name would be Pearl Milling Company. PepsiCo purchased that brand name for that purpose on February 1, 2021.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-cnn_2021-02-06-7) The new branding was launched that June, one year after the company announced that they would drop Aunt Jemima branding. PepsiCo referenced the Aunt Jemima brand by [logotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logotype "Logotype") on the front of the packaging for at least six months after the rebrand. Following that period, PepsiCo said that it wouldn't be able to completely and permanently abandon the Aunt Jemima brand due to [trademark law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trademark_law "Trademark law"); if it did, a third party could obtain and use the brand.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-fortune_2021-02-11-5)

## Character of Aunt Jemima

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Character of Aunt Jemima")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/JemimasWeddingDay.jpg/250px-JemimasWeddingDay.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JemimasWeddingDay.jpg)

"Jemima" character on 1899 [cakewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cakewalk "Cakewalk") sheet music cover

Aunt Jemima is based on the common [enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States")["Mammy" archetype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammy_archetype_in_the_United_States "Mammy archetype in the United States"), a plump black woman wearing a headscarf who is a devoted and submissive servant.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2015-06-24-18) Her skin is dark and dewy, with a pearly-white smile. Although depictions vary over time, they are similar to the common attire and physical features of "mammy" characters throughout American history.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Atlantic_2012-04-23-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-fortune_2014-08-12-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NWHM-33)[_[excessive citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources#Bundling\_citations "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

The terms "aunt" and "uncle" in this context were a [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") form of address used with older enslaved persons. They were denied use of [English honorifics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_honorifics "English honorifics"), such as "mistress" and "mister", respectively.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Berry_2020-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-prmuseum-35)

A British image in the Library of Congress, which may have been created as early as 1847, shows a smiling black woman named "Miss Jim-Ima Crow", with a framed image of "[James Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws "Jim Crow laws")" on the wall behind her.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-36) A character named "Aunt Jemima" appeared on the stage in Washington, D.C., as early as 1864.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-37) Rutt's inspiration for Aunt Jemima was [Billy Kersands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Kersands "Billy Kersands")'s American-style [minstrelsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minstrel_show "Minstrel show")/[vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") song "[Old Aunt Jemima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Aunt_Jemima "Old Aunt Jemima")", written in 1875. Rutt reportedly saw a minstrel show featuring the "Old Aunt Jemima" song in the fall of 1889, presented by [blackface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackface "Blackface") performers identified by Arthur F. Marquette as "Baker & Farrell".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13) Marquette recounts that the actor playing Aunt Jemima wore an [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apron "Apron") and [kerchief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerchief "Kerchief").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-prmuseum-35)

However, Doris Witt at [University of Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Iowa "University of Iowa") was unable to confirm Marquette's account.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14) Witt suggests that Rutt might have witnessed a performance by the vaudeville performer Pete F. Baker, who played characters described in newspapers of that era as "Ludwig" and "Aunt Jemima". His portrayal of the Aunt Jemima character may have been a white male in blackface, pretending to be a German immigrant imitating a black minstrel parodying an imaginary black female enslaved cook.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)

### Advertising

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Advertising")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/New-York_tribune.%2C_November_07%2C_1909%2C_Page_20%2C_Image_44_Aunt_Jemima.jpg/250px-New-York_tribune.%2C_November_07%2C_1909%2C_Page_20%2C_Image_44_Aunt_Jemima.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New-York_tribune.,_November_07,_1909,_Page_20,_Image_44_Aunt_Jemima.jpg)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Aunt_Jemima_Pancake_Flour%2C_1935.jpg/120px-Aunt_Jemima_Pancake_Flour%2C_1935.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aunt_Jemima_Pancake_Flour,_1935.jpg)

1935 Quaker Oats magazine advertisement for Aunt Jemima pancake mix, featuring Anna Robinson as Aunt Jemima

Marketing materials for the line of products centered around the "Mammy" archetype, including the slogan first used at the 1893 [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in Chicago, Illinois: "I's in Town, Honey".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38)

At that World's Fair, and for decades afterward,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-prmuseum-35) marketers created and circulated fictional stories about Aunt Jemima.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9) She was presented as a "loyal cook" for a fictional Colonel Higbee's [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") plantation on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-40) Jemima was said to use a secret recipe "from the South before the Civil War", with their "matchless plantation flavor", to make the best pancakes in [Dixie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixie "Dixie").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-prmuseum-35)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) Another story described her as diverting Union soldiers during the Civil War with her pancakes long enough for Colonel Higbee to escape.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38) She was said to have revived a group of shipwrecked survivors with her flapjacks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9)

Beginning in 1894, the company added an Aunt Jemima paper doll family that could be cut out from the pancake box.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) Aunt Jemima is joined by her husband, Uncle [Rastus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastus "Rastus") (later renamed Uncle Mose to avoid confusion with the [Cream of Wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_of_Wheat "Cream of Wheat") character, while Uncle Mose was first introduced as the plantation butler).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-41) Their children, described as "comical pickaninnies", were named Abraham Lincoln, Dilsie, Zeb, and Dinah. The paper-doll family was posed dancing barefoot and dressed in tattered clothing, and the box was labeled "Before the Receipt was sold". ([Receipt](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/receipt "wikt:receipt") is an archaic rural form of recipe.)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) Buying another box with elegant clothing cut-outs to fit over the dolls, the customer could transform them "After the Receipt was sold". This placed them in the [Horatio Alger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Alger "Horatio Alger") rags-to-riches American cultural mythos.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)

[Rag-doll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rag_doll "Rag doll") versions were offered as a premium in 1909: "Aunt Jemima Pancake Flour / Pica ninny Doll / The Davis Milling Company". Early versions were portrayed as poor people with patches on their trousers, large mouths, and missing teeth. The children's names were changed to Diana and Wade. Over time, there were improvements in appearance. Oil-cloth versions were available circa the 1950s, with cartoonish features, round eyes, and watermelon mouths.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-42)

A typical magazine ad from the turn of the century created by advertising executive [James Webb Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Young "James Webb Young") and the illustrator [N.C. Wyeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N.C._Wyeth "N.C. Wyeth")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38) shows a heavyset black cook talking happily while a white man takes notes. The ad copy says, "After the Civil War, after her master's death, Aunt Jemima was finally persuaded to sell her famous pancake recipe to the representative of a northern milling company."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9)

However, the Davis Milling Company was not located in a Northern state: [Missouri in the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_in_the_American_Civil_War "Missouri in the American Civil War") was a hotly contested [border state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_states_(American_Civil_War) "Border states (American Civil War)"). In reality, Aunt Jemima never existed, created by marketers to better sell products.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NWHM-33)

### Controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Controversy")]

See also: [Nadir of American race relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir_of_American_race_relations "Nadir of American race relations")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/The_Saturday_evening_post_%281920%29_%2814598409868%29.jpg/250px-The_Saturday_evening_post_%281920%29_%2814598409868%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Saturday_evening_post_(1920)_(14598409868).jpg)

1920 _Saturday Evening Post_ ad with N.C. Wyeth illustration

Although the Aunt Jemima character was not created until nearly 25 years after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the clothing, dancing, enslaved dialect, and singing old plantation songs as she worked, all harkened back to a glorified view of [antebellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_South "Antebellum South") Southern plantation life as a "[happy slave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_slave "Happy slave")" narrative.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NWHM-33)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) The marketing legend surrounding Aunt Jemima's successful commercialization of her "secret recipe" contributed to the post-Civil War nostalgia and romanticism of Southern life in service of America's developing consumer culture—especially in the context of selling kitchen items.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2015-06-24-18)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Atlantic_2012-04-23-31)

African-American women formed the Women's Columbian Association and the Women's Columbian Auxiliary Association to address the exclusion of African Americans from the 1893 [World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") exhibitions, asking that the fair reflect the success of post-Emancipation African Americans.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) Instead, the Fair included a miniature West African village whose natives were portrayed as primitive savages.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38)[Ida B. Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_B._Wells "Ida B. Wells") was incensed by the exclusion of African Americans from mainstream fair activities; the so-called "Negro Day" was a picnic held off-site from the fairgrounds.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)

Black scholars [Hallie Quinn Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallie_Quinn_Brown "Hallie Quinn Brown"), [Anna Julia Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Julia_Cooper "Anna Julia Cooper"), and [Fannie Barrier Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fannie_Barrier_Williams "Fannie Barrier Williams") used the World's Fair as an opportunity to address how African-American women were being exploited by white men.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-43) In her book _A Voice from the South_ (1892), Cooper had noted the fascination with "Southern influence, Southern ideas, and Southern ideals" had "dictated to and domineered over the brain and sinew of this nation".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)

These educated progressive women saw "a mammy for the national household" represented at the World's Fair by Aunt Jemima, according to Professor Kimberly Wallace-Sanders of Emory University.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) The women argued that this directly relates to the belief that slavery cultivated innate qualities in African Americans. According to them, the notion that African Americans were natural servants reinforced a racist ideology renouncing the reality of African American intellect.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) These women also contended that Aunt Jemima embodied a post-Reconstruction fantasy of idealized domesticity, inspired by "happy slave" hospitality, and revealed a deep need to redeem the antebellum South.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39) There were others that capitalized on this theme, such as [Uncle Ben's Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Ben's_Rice "Uncle Ben's Rice") and [Cream of Wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_of_Wheat "Cream of Wheat")'s Rastus.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-prmuseum-35)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-KWS_1962-39)

### Slang

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Slang")]

The term "Aunt Jemima" is sometimes used colloquially as a female version of the derogatory epithet "[Uncle Tom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Tom "Uncle Tom")" or "[Rastus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastus "Rastus")". In this context, the slang term "Aunt Jemima" falls within the "[mammy archetype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammy_archetype "Mammy archetype")" and refers to a friendly black woman who is perceived as obsequiously servile or acting in, or protective of, the interests of [whites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Americans "White Americans").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-44)

John Sylvester of [WTDY-AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WOZN_(AM) "WOZN (AM)") drew criticism after calling [Condoleezza Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condoleezza_Rice "Condoleezza Rice") an "Aunt Jemima" and [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell") an "Uncle Tom", referring to remarks by singer and civil rights activist [Harry Belafonte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Belafonte "Harry Belafonte") about their alleged subservience in the [George W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_administration "George W. Bush administration"). He apologized by giving away Aunt Jemima's pancake mix and syrup.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-45)

Barry Presgraves, then 77-year-old Mayor of [Luray, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luray,_Virginia "Luray, Virginia"), was [censured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censure_in_the_United_States "Censure in the United States") 5-to-1 by the town council because he referred to [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") as "Aunt Jemima" after she was selected by [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") to be the [Democratic Party vice presidential candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2020 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-49)

## Performers of Aunt Jemima

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Performers of Aunt Jemima")]

The African American Registry of the United States suggests [Nancy Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Green "Nancy Green") and others who played the caricature of Aunt Jemima[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-forbes_2020-06-17-24) should be celebrated despite what has been widely condemned as a stereotypical and racist brand image. The registry wrote, "We celebrate the birth of Nancy Green in 1834. She was a Black storyteller and one of the first Black corporate models in the United States."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-50)

Following Green's work as Aunt Jemima, very few were well known. Advertising agencies (such as [J. Walter Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Walter_Thompson "J. Walter Thompson"), [Lord and Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draftfcb "Draftfcb"), and others) hired dozens of actors to portray the role, often assigned regionally, as the first organized sales promotion campaign.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9)

Quaker Oats ended local appearances for Aunt Jemima in 1965.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Buckley_2020-51)

### Nancy Green

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Nancy Green")]

Main article: [Nancy Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Green "Nancy Green")

Nancy Green was the first spokesperson hired by the R. T. Davis Milling Company for the Aunt Jemima pancake mix.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-history_2007-08-23-2) Green was born into slavery in [Montgomery County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_County,_Kentucky "Montgomery County, Kentucky"), Kentucky.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-courier_2020-06-17-52) Dressed as Aunt Jemima, Green appeared at the 1893 [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in Chicago, beside the "world's largest flour barrel" (24 feet high), where she operated a pancake-cooking display, sang songs, and told romanticized stories about the Old South (a happy place for blacks and whites alike). She appeared at fairs, festivals, flea markets, food shows, and local grocery stores, her arrival heralded by large billboards featuring the caption, "I'se in town, honey."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-caricature_mammy-3)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-courier_2020-06-17-52)

Green refused to cross the Atlantic Ocean for the [1900 Paris exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1900) "Exposition Universelle (1900)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Nagasawa_2020-53) She was replaced by Agnes Moody. Green died in 1923 and was buried in an unmarked pauper's grave in Chicago's [Oak Woods Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Woods_Cemetery "Oak Woods Cemetery").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NYT_2020-07-17-38)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Nagasawa_2020-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crowther_2020-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Defender_2020-08-31-55) A headstone was placed on September 5, 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crusader_2020-09-15-56)

### Agnes Moody

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Agnes Moody")]

60-year-old Agnes Moody first performed as Aunt Jemima at the [1900 Paris exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1900) "Exposition Universelle (1900)"), and was erroneously reported as the original Aunt Jemima.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-IDR_1900-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-PG_1903-04-10-58) She had become well known in the Chicago area for her cornmeal bread and cakes. She died April 9, 1903.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-PG_1903-04-10-58)

### Lillian Richard

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Lillian Richard")]

Main article: [Lillian Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Richard "Lillian Richard")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Lillian_Richard_Historical_Marker.png/250px-Lillian_Richard_Historical_Marker.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lillian_Richard_Historical_Marker.png)

Historical marker dedicated to Lillian Richard, Aunt Jemima portrayer

Lillian Richard was hired to portray Aunt Jemima in 1925, and she remained in the role for 23 years. Richard was born in 1891, and grew up in the tiny community of [Fouke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fouke,_Texas "Fouke, Texas") seven miles west of [Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkins,_Texas "Hawkins, Texas") in [Wood County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_County,_Texas "Wood County, Texas"), Texas. In 1910, she moved to [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), working initially as a cook. Her job "pitching pancakes" was based in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_Texas "Paris, Texas"), Texas.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9) After she suffered a stroke _circa_ 1947–1948, she returned to Fouke, where she lived until her death in 1956. Richard was honored with a [Texas Historical Marker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Historical_Marker "Texas Historical Marker") in her hometown, dedicated in her name on June 30, 2012.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-TM_2002-10-01-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-62)

[Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkins,_Texas "Hawkins, Texas"), Texas, east of [Mineola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineola,_Texas "Mineola, Texas"), is known as the "Pancake Capital of Texas" because of longtime resident Lillian Richard. The local chamber of commerce decided to use Hawkins's connection to Aunt Jemima to boost tourism.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-TM_2002-10-01-59) In 1995, state senator David Cain introduced Senate Resolution No. 73 designating Hawkins as the "Pancake Capital of Texas", which was passed into law; the measure was spearheaded by Lillian's niece, Jewell Richard-McCalla.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Crocker_1996-9)

### Anna Robinson

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Anna Robinson")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Anna_Robinson_as_Aunt_Jemima.jpg/250px-Anna_Robinson_as_Aunt_Jemima.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anna_Robinson_as_Aunt_Jemima.jpg)

Anna Robinson as Aunt Jemima in an advertisement

Anna Robinson was hired to play Aunt Jemima at the 1933 [Century of Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_of_Progress "Century of Progress") Chicago World's Fair.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-history_2007-08-23-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13) Robinson answered an open audition, and her appearance was more like the "mammy" stereotype than the slender Lillian Richard.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14) Born circa 1899, she was also from Kentucky and widowed (like Green), but in her thirties, with eight years of education.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64) She was sent to New York City by [Lord and Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCB_(advertising_agency) "FCB (advertising agency)") to have her picture taken. A 1967 company history commemorated this journey as "the day they loaded 350 pounds of Anna Robinson on the Twentieth Century Limited."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13)

She appeared at prestigious establishments frequented by the rich and famous, such as [El Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Morocco "El Morocco"), the [Stork Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stork_Club "Stork Club"), "[21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_Club "21 Club")", and the [Waldorf-Astoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldorf-Astoria "Waldorf-Astoria").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64) Photos show Robinson making pancakes for celebrities and stars of [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre"), radio, and motion pictures. They were used in advertising "ranked among the highest read of their time".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-marquette-13) The Aunt Jemima packaging was redesigned in her likeness.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BlackHunger-14)

Robinson reportedly worked for the company until her death in 1951; however,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-history_2007-08-23-2) the work, which was sporadic and for mere weeks in a year,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64) was not enough to escape the hard life into which she had been born.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64) Her $1,200 total payment in 1939 (equivalent to $27,775 in 2025) was almost the entirety of the household's annual income[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64) and stood in stark contrast to the official Aunt Jemima history timeline, which stated that Robinson was "able to make enough money to provide for her children and buy a 22-room house where she rents rooms to boarders".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-history_2020-06-28-65) The same claim was made for [Anna Short Harrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Short_Harrington "Anna Short Harrington"), yet, according to the 1940 census, she rented an apartment in a four-flat in [Washington Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Park_(community_area),_Chicago "Washington Park (community area), Chicago") with her daughter, son-in-law, and two grandchildren.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Hansen_2020-64)

### Rosa Washington Riles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Rosa Washington Riles")]

Rosa Washington Riles became the third face on Aunt Jemima packaging in the 1930s, and continued until 1948. Rosa Washington was born in 1901 near [Red Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redoak,_Ohio "Redoak, Ohio") in [Brown County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Ohio "Brown County, Ohio"), Ohio, one of several children of Robert and Julie (Holliday) Washington and a granddaughter of George and Phoeba Washington.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Tucker_2001-66) She was employed as a cook in the home of a Quaker Oats executive and began pancake demonstrations at her employer's request. She died in 1969, and is buried near her parents and grandparents in the historic [Red Oak Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Oak_Presbyterian_Church "Red Oak Presbyterian Church") cemetery of [Ripley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripley,_Ohio "Ripley, Ohio"), Ohio.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Tucker_2001-66) An annual Aunt Jemima breakfast has been a long-time fundraiser for the cemetery, and the church maintains a collection of Aunt Jemima memorabilia.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Berry_2020-34)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Tucker_2001-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-68)

### Anna Short Harrington

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Anna Short Harrington")]

Main article: [Anna Short Harrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Short_Harrington "Anna Short Harrington")

Anna Short Harrington began her career as Aunt Jemima in 1935 and continued to play the role until 1954. She was born in 1897 in [Marlboro County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlboro_County,_South_Carolina "Marlboro County, South Carolina"), South Carolina. The Short family lived on the [Pegues Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegues_Place "Pegues Place") plantation as sharecroppers.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Sloan_2009-69) In 1927, she moved to [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_New_York "Syracuse, New York"), New York. Quaker Oats discovered her cooking pancakes at the 1935 [New York State Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Fair "New York State Fair").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Case_2002-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Wight_2020-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Croyle_2020-72) Harrington died in Syracuse in 1955.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Sloan_2009-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Case_2002-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Wight_2020-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Croyle_2020-72)

### Ethel Ernestine Harper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Ethel Ernestine Harper")]

Main article: [Ethel Ernestine Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethel_Ernestine_Harper "Ethel Ernestine Harper")

Ethel Ernestine Harper portrayed Aunt Jemima during the 1950s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-BIA-1)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Ingrano_2019-21) Harper was born on September 17, 1903, in [Greensboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro,_Alabama "Greensboro, Alabama"), Alabama.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-74) After graduating from college at the age of 17, she taught elementary school for 2 years and high school mathematics for 10 years. ### Rosie Lee Moore Hall

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Rosie Lee Moore Hall")]

Rosie Lee Moore Hall, the last "living" Aunt Jemima, was born in [Robertson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson_County,_Texas "Robertson County, Texas"), Texas on June 22, 1899. ## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aunt_Jemima&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Aunt Jemima has been featured in various formats and settings throughout popular culture. Aunt Jemima has been a present image identifiable by popular culture for well over a century, dating back to Nancy Green's appearance at the [1893 World Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in Chicago, Illinois.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-76)

_Aunt Jemima_, a minstrel-type variety radio program, was broadcast January 17, 1929 – June 5, 1953, at times on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and at other times on the [Blue Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Network "Blue Network"). The program had several hiatuses during its time on the air.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Dunning-77)

In the 1960s, [Betye Saar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betye_Saar "Betye Saar") began collecting images of Aunt Jemima, [Uncle Tom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Tom "Uncle Tom"), [Little Black Sambo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Black_Sambo "Little Black Sambo"), and other stereotyped African-American figures from folk culture and advertising of the [Jim Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws "Jim Crow laws") era. She incorporated them into collages and assemblages, transforming them into statements of political and social protest.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Britannica-78)_The Liberation of Aunt Jemima_ is one of her most notable works from this era. In this mixed-media assemblage, Saar utilized the stereotypical [mammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammy_archetype "Mammy archetype") figure of Aunt Jemima to subvert traditional notions of race and gender.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-NPR-79)

"Aunt Jemima's Kitchen"—named Aunt Jemima's Pancake House when it first started operating in 1955—was a restaurant opened in 1962 during the Civil Rights Movement as the official Aunt Jemima restaurant at [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland"). In addition to the restaurant, a woman portraying Aunt Jemima was poised at the restaurant to take pictures with its patrons.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-80) Aunt Jemima's Kitchen also had additional locations across the United States.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-81) However, the Disneyland location closed in July 1970 after Quaker Oats withdrew its sponsorship following a dispute with [The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") over control of the restaurant.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-82)

The Aunt Jemima character, portrayed at the time by [Edith Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Wilson_(singer) "Edith Wilson (singer)"), received the [Key to the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_to_the_City "Key to the City") of [Albion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albion,_Michigan "Albion, Michigan"), Michigan, on January 25, 1964.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-83) Actresses portraying Aunt Jemima visited Albion, [Battle Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_Creek,_Michigan "Battle Creek, Michigan") ("Cereal City"), and other Michigan cities many times over three decades. [Grand Rapids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Rapids,_Michigan "Grand Rapids, Michigan") had an Aunt Jemima's Kitchen, one of 21 locations, until it was changed to Colonial Kitchen in 1968.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-Buckley_2020-51)

[Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") includes a song titled "[Electric Aunt Jemima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_Aunt_Jemima "Electric Aunt Jemima")" on his 1969 album _[Uncle Meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Meat "Uncle Meat")_. Electric Aunt Jemima was the nickname for Zappa's [Standel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standel "Standel") guitar amplifier.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-84)

[Faith Ringgold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Ringgold "Faith Ringgold")'s first quilt story _[Who's Afraid of Aunt Jemima?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who's\_Afraid\_of\_Aunt\_Jemima%3F "Who's Afraid of Aunt Jemima?")_ (1983) depicts the story of Aunt Jemima as a matriarch restaurateur. Through mediums of text and imagery used to characterize Aunt Jemima in the public sphere, Ringgold represented the oppressed mammy caricature as an entrepreneur.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunt_Jemima#cite_note-85)

**Denali** ([/d ə ˈ n ɑː l i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_də-NAH-lee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-5)[Koyukon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyukon_language "Koyukon language"): _Deenaalee_), federally designated as **Mount McKinley**,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-Friedman2025-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-7) is the highest [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") peak in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), with a summit [elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevation "Elevation") of 20,310 feet (6,190 m) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). Its vertical relief above the surrounding plateaus is one of the greatest on Earth, measuring about 18,000 feet (5,500 meters).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-Helman2005-8) With a [topographic prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_prominence "Topographic prominence") of 20,156 feet (6,144 m)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-PeakVisor-3) and a [topographic isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographic_isolation "Topographic isolation") of 4,621.1 miles (7,436.9 km),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-PeakVisor-3) Denali is the [third most prominent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_peaks_by_prominence "List of peaks by prominence") and [third-most isolated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_peaks_by_isolation "List of peaks by isolation") peak on Earth, after [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") and [Aconcagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aconcagua "Aconcagua"). Located in the [Alaska Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Range "Alaska Range") in the interior of the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), Denali is the centerpiece of [Denali National Park and Preserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali_National_Park_and_Preserve "Denali National Park and Preserve").

The [Koyukon people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyukon_people "Koyukon people") who inhabit the area around the mountain have referred to the peak as "Denali" for centuries. In 1896, a gold prospector named it "Mount McKinley" in support of then presidential candidate [William McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley"), who later became the 25th president; McKinley's name was the official name recognized by the [federal government of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") from 1917 until 2015. In 1975, the [State of Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Alaska "State of Alaska") officially renamed the mountain Denali and requested the federal government follow suit. The [United States Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior") changed the [official federal name of the mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali%E2%80%93Mount_McKinley_naming_dispute "Denali–Mount McKinley naming dispute") to Denali on August 29, 2015.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-DenaliNameChangeDOI-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-denalirestored-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-McKinley_Name-11) In January 2025, the Department of the Interior under the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump") reverted the mountain's official federal name to Mount McKinley.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-:8-12)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-Friedman2025-6)

In 1903, [James Wickersham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wickersham "James Wickersham") recorded the first attempt at climbing Denali, which was unsuccessful. In 1906, [Frederick Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Cook "Frederick Cook") claimed the [first ascent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_ascent "First ascent"), but this ascent is unverified and its legitimacy questioned. The first verifiable ascent to Denali's summit was achieved on June 7, 1913, by climbers [Hudson Stuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Stuck "Hudson Stuck"), [Harry Karstens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Karstens "Harry Karstens"), [Walter Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Harper "Walter Harper"), and [Robert Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Tatum "Robert Tatum"), who went by the South Summit. In 1951, [Bradford Washburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford_Washburn "Bradford Washburn") pioneered the West Buttress route, considered to be the safest and easiest route, and therefore the most popular.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-roberts-13)

On September 2, 2015, the [U.S. Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Geological_Survey "U.S. Geological Survey") measured the mountain at 20,310 feet (6,190 m) high,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-ADN-1) 10 ft lower than the 20,320 feet (6,194 m) measured in 1952 using [photogrammetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photogrammetry "Photogrammetry").

## Geology and features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Denali&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geology and features")]

Denali is a [granitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granitic "Granitic")[pluton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluton "Pluton"), mostly pink [quartz monzonite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz_monzonite "Quartz monzonite"), lifted by [tectonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic "Tectonic") pressure from the [subduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") of the [Pacific plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_plate "Pacific plate") beneath the [North American plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_plate "North American plate"); at the same time, the [sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary "Sedimentary") material above and around the mountain was stripped away by [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion "Erosion").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-brease-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-15) The forces that lifted Denali also caused many deep [earthquakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake") in Alaska and the [Aleutian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleutian_Islands "Aleutian Islands"). The Pacific Plate is seismically active beneath Denali, a tectonic region that is known as the "McKinley cluster".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-hanson-16)

### Structural geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Denali&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Structural geology")]

The high topography of Denali is related to the complex structural relationships created by the right-lateral [Denali Fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali_Fault "Denali Fault") and Denali Fault Bend. The Denali Fault is caused by stresses created by the low-angle subduction of the [Yakutat microplate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutat_Block "Yakutat Block") underneath Alaska. The Denali Fault Bend is characterized as a gentle restraining bend.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-:3-17) The Denali Fault Bend represents a curvature in the Denali Fault that is approximately 75 km long. This curvature creates what is known as a "space problem". As the right-lateral movement along the Denali Fault continues, high compressional forces created at the fault bend essentially push the crust up in a vertical fashion. The longer the crust stays within the restraining bend, the higher the topography will be. Several active normal faults north of the restraining bend have recently been mapped with slip rates of approximately 2–6 mm/year.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-:3-17) These normal faults help to accommodate the unusual curvature of the restraining bend.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Elevation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Denali&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Elevation")]

Denali has a summit [elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevation "Elevation") of 20,310 feet (6,190 m) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), making it the highest peak in North America and the northernmost mountain above 19,685 feet (6,000 m) elevation in the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-ADN-1) Measured from base to peak at some 18,000 ft (5,500 m), it is among the largest mountains situated entirely above sea level. Denali rises from a sloping plain with elevations from 1,000 to 3,000 ft (300 to 910 m), for a base-to-peak height of 17,000 to 19,000 ft (5,000 to 6,000 m).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-18) By comparison, [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") rises from the [Tibetan Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Plateau "Tibetan Plateau") at a much higher base elevation. Base elevations for Everest range from 13,800 ft (4,200 m) on the south side to 17,100 ft (5,200 m) on the Tibetan Plateau, for a base-to-peak height in the range of 12,000 to 15,300 ft (3,700 to 4,700 m).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-washburn_map-19) Denali's base-to-peak height is little more than half the 33,500 ft (10,200 m) of the volcano [Mauna Kea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauna_Kea "Mauna Kea"), which lies mostly under water.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-natgeo-20)

### Geography of the mountain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Denali&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Geography of the mountain")]

Denali has two significant summits: the South Summit is the higher one, while the North Summit has an elevation of 19,470 ft (5,934 m)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-brease-14) and a [prominence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prominence "Prominence") of approximately 1,270 ft (387 m).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-pbnorth-21) The North Summit is sometimes counted as a separate peak (see e.g., [fourteener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourteener "Fourteener")) and sometimes not; it is rarely climbed, except by those doing routes on the north side of the [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif").

Five large glaciers flow off the slopes of the mountain. The [Peters Glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peters_Glacier_(Alaska_Range) "Peters Glacier (Alaska Range)") lies on the northwest side of the massif, while the [Muldrow Glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muldrow_Glacier "Muldrow Glacier") falls from its northeast slopes. Just to the east of the Muldrow, and abutting the eastern side of the massif, is the [Traleika Glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traleika_Glacier "Traleika Glacier"). The [Ruth Glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Glacier "Ruth Glacier") lies to the southeast of the mountain, and the [Kahiltna Glacier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahiltna_Glacier "Kahiltna Glacier") leads up to the southwest side of the mountain.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-areaparks-22)[_[new archival link needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Archiving\_a\_source "Help:Archiving a source")_][[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-planetware-23) With a length of 44 mi (71 km), the Kahiltna Glacier is the longest glacier in the [Alaska Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Range "Alaska Range").

### William A. Dickey

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Denali&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: William A. Dickey")]

In 1896, gold prospector William Dickey[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-Brooks1911-29) named it _McKinley_ as political support for then-presidential candidate [William McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley"), who became president the following year.

> One, however, W. A. Dickey, of a different type from the rest, recognized the surpassing height of the peak and its geographic import and gave it the name Mount McKinley. His exploration in 1896 was probably one of the first extensive journeys in this district since that of the Russian Malakoff in 1834. With three other men he ascended Susitna River to the trading station at the head of the delta; then constructed boats of whipsawed lumber and continued his journey up the main Susitna to the mouth of Indian Creek. From this place he explored a part of the upper canyon of the Susitna and also made a journey westward to the Chulitna, reaching the foot of the glacier which discharges into this river and has its source on the slopes of Mount McKinley. It was after this journey that he published his description of the mountain, in which he named it and stated its altitude as over 20,000 feet. He told the writer that he had no instruments, but made his estimate, which has proved to be remarkably accurate, with careful consideration of the atmospheric conditions, as well as of the probable distance to the base of the peak. In 1897 he made a second trip into this region, with one companion, and extended his previous explorations. He was the first to call attention to the great lowland drained by Tokichitna River and to the low divide which separates it from the Kuskokwim drainage, later explored by Spurr, Herron, and the writer.

—[Alfred H. Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hulse_Brooks "Alfred Hulse Brooks"), "The Mount McKinley Region, Alaska", _Department of the Interior, United States Geological Survey, Professional Paper 70_[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-Brooks1911-29)

The United States formally recognized the name Mount McKinley after President [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson") signed the Mount McKinley National Park Act of February 26, 1917.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-30) In 1965, President [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson") declared the north and south peaks of the mountain the "Churchill Peaks", in honor of British statesman [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-31) The Alaska Board of Geographic Names changed the state name of the mountain to _Denali_ in 1975, which was how it was referred to locally.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-McKinley_Name-11)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-32) However, a request in 1975 from the Alaska state legislature to the [United States Board on Geographic Names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Board_on_Geographic_Names "United States Board on Geographic Names") to do the same at the federal level was blocked by Ohio congressman [Ralph Regula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Regula "Ralph Regula"), whose district included McKinley's home town of [Canton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Ohio "Canton, Ohio").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-monmonier-33)

[Hudson Stuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Stuck "Hudson Stuck"), the organizer of the Stuck-Karstens Expedition, which was the first confirmed team to summit the mountain, preferred the name Denali over McKinley, referring to it as Denali nearly exclusively in his account of the expedition.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStuck1914vii-47)

According to the [Alaska Department of Commerce, Community, and Economic Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Department_of_Commerce,_Community,_and_Economic_Development "Alaska Department of Commerce, Community, and Economic Development")'s official database of [business licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_license "Business license"), businesses named after Denali outnumber those named after McKinley by a margin of six to one.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-48)

Indigenous names for Denali can be found in seven different Alaskan languages. The names fall into two categories. To the south of the Alaska Range in the [Dena'ina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dena'ina_language "Dena'ina language") and [Ahtna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahtna_language "Ahtna language") languages the mountain is known by names that are translated as 'big mountain'. To the north of the Alaska Range in the [Lower Tanana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Tanana_language "Lower Tanana language"), [Koyukon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyukon_language "Koyukon language"), [Upper Kuskokwim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Kuskokwim_language "Upper Kuskokwim language"), [Holikachuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holikachuk_language "Holikachuk language"), and [Deg Xinag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deg_Xinag_language "Deg Xinag language") languages the mountain is known by names that are translated as 'the high one',[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-49) 'the tall one' (Koyukon, Lower and Middle Tanana, Upper Kuskokwim, Deg Xinag, and Holikachuk).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-karijamden-50)

Asked about the importance of the mountain and its name, Will Mayo, former president of the [Tanana Chiefs Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanana_Chiefs_Conference "Tanana Chiefs Conference"), an organization that represents 42 Athabaskan tribes in the Alaskan interior, said: "It's not one homogeneous belief structure around the mountain, but we all agree that we're all deeply gratified by the acknowledgment of the importance of Denali to Alaska's people."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali#cite_note-mayochiefsconference-51)
